Electricity: Geometric Power puts Aba ahead of Nigerian cities
items.description: By Emma Ujah, Abuja Bureau Chief For decades, unreliable electricity supply has undermined Nigeria’s industrial growth, forcing businesses to close, driving up production costs and making life increasingly difficult for households. From textile mills in Kaduna, Kano, Lagos and Onitsha to vehicle assembly plants, tyre factories and footwear manufacturers, several once-thriving industries have struggled or shut down, partly because of inadequate power supply. Now in Aba, Abia State, a different experience is emerging, as the Geometric Power-owned Aba Power distribution network provides electricity to businesses, institutions and households, enabling some to reduce dependence on costly petrol and diesel generators. The development is reshaping business operations in the commercial hub, with manufacturers reporting uninterrupted production, traders extending working hours and households enjoying improved food preservation and lower running costs. Geometric Power Chairman, Professor Barth Nnaji, described the Aba Integrated Power Project, an investment exceeding $900 million, as a dream come true. He said the company was committed to providing reliable and affordable electricity to customers, irrespective of their social or economic status. “Our services are for all people, regardless of class or status. Electricity is a fundamental right of the Nigerian people, and we are happy to provide reliable and affordable electricity to all our customers,” Nnaji said. He added that, unlike other legacy distribution companies, Aba Power was wholly privately owned and had not received Federal Government subsidies. Role of Afreximbank The decision of the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank) to provide a $50 million facility to Geometric Power Limited after a seven-year delay was what made Aba Power a reality today. The Group Managing Director of Geometric Power, Mrs. Agatha Nnaji, said the bank provided the lifeline that enabled the project to be commissioned, saying, “Afreximbank is the bank that provided the funding that enabled us to complete and commission the project.” “As you may know, politics got in the way, human error impacted the project, and it was delayed just as we were about to commission it. So, for seven years, we were simply maintaining the facilities that were already in place. We had staff who had to be paid to keep maintaining them. “Eventually, when we determined the exact amount needed to complete the project—after President Jonathan intervened and his successor, the late President Muhammadu Buhari, directed his team to resolve the issues arising from the privatization—we were thrilled that Afreximbank stepped in. They shared our vision and understood the impact the project would have on the community. “I believe that was the turning point for them. Seeing Aba’s potential as an industrial hub in Africa made them far more willing to find a way to make the project work. Although subsequent challenges prolonged completion, Afreximbank ultimately came to the rescue. “At that crucial juncture, we needed $50 million, and they provided it. Honestly, Afreximbank’s role in all of this was remarkable. Ordinarily, a bank or financier would walk away from a project facing the kinds of hurdles we had at the time. “We were operating in an environment where the government had breached the terms of our signed agreement. We were dealing with civil and public service officials who knew what needed to be done but refused to act. “There was little to offer them comfort beyond the sheer determination of our lead investor. For him, it wasn’t merely a financial venture; his drive to see the project through was fueled by a desire to create a lasting, positive impact on people’s lives.” Infrastructure built for reliability The company says its investment in distribution infrastructure is central to its efforts to maintain stable electricity supply. According to the Director of Commercial Operations, Engineer Victor Ngwoke, Aba Power deliberately invested in heavy-duty tubular steel poles designed to withstand extreme conditions and minimise disruptions. “We wanted to have a very sturdy and reliable infrastructure. We, therefore, deliberately invested in heavy tubular steel poles,” he said. Ngwoke explained that the poles have deeply buried concrete foundations and are designed to withstand substantial impact, including collisions with vehicles. He said the company also maintained standards for conventional concrete poles and worked to restore damaged infrastructure quickly whenever faults occurred. On metering, the director said approximately 98 per cent of Aba Power’s customers had prepaid meters, helping to reduce disputes associated with estimated billing. With prepaid meters, customers can monitor their consumption and manage electricity expenses more effectively. Ngwoke also disclosed that the company deployed smart meters and monitoring teams to detect and prevent electricity theft, including illegal connections and meter bypasses. He said residents had also supported efforts to protect the network, recognising the benefits of reliable electricity to their businesses and livelihoods. Excess capacity, wider reach Aba Power currently takes an average of 50 to 60 megawatts from an installed generation capacity exceeding 140MW, according to the company. The available capacity has enabled it to extend electricity supply to parts of neighbouring Rivers State, where some communities are underserved by the Port Harcourt Electricity Distribution Company. The company says it hopes to extend its reach across Abia State, subject to the necessary infrastructure and operational requirements. Polytechnic cuts energy costs by 80% One of the institutions benefiting from the improved supply is Ogbonnaya Onu Polytechnic, Aba, whose Rector, Professor Christopher Okoro, said the development had transformed academic and administrative activities. Okoro, who assumed office in 2024, said one of the first challenges he encountered was a huge outstanding diesel bill, which he considered unsustainable. He contacted Nnaji for assistance, and the institution was connected to Aba Power within 48 hours. Before the connection, he said, academic activities, research and other operations were constrained by unreliable electricity, with staff often leaving the campus by 2pm. With the improved supply, students and staff now remain on campus until late in the evening, despite the institution not being residential. “Before now, staff used to leave by 2pm. They cannot work without electricity. You cannot carry out research without electricity,” he said. The rector said the institution’s energy costs had fallen by about 80 per cent. Manufacturers, traders extend working hours At Damson Industries, a manufacturer of shoe components, Chairman David Mmadueke, said reliable electricity had enabled the company to operate day and night shifts without routinely shutting down because of power outages. “We have light here morning and night. The only time we didn’t have light was when the company had a problem with gas supply for about three days. Apart from that, this factory has never closed because there is no electricity,” he said. Similarly, the President of Aba North Shoe Plaza, Obioma Onyebuchi, said the plaza, which houses more than 2,000 shops, switched to Aba Power on January 14 and had since enjoyed steady supply. According to him, traders no longer depend on individual petrol or diesel generators, as the company has ensured that customers are metered. “With the constant electricity supply from Aba Power, we can now work throughout the day. This has increased the productivity of our members,” he said. Although some traders consider the electricity tariff high, Onyebuchi said the cost remained preferable to the substantial sums previously spent on fuel. He expressed the plaza’s readiness to support the company to sustain reliable supply. Steady power eases household expenses Beyond factories and commercial centres, improved electricity supply is also changing how some households manage their finances. Mrs Ada-Ngizi Greg-Ilobinso, a wife, mother and teacher, said reliable electricity had made household management easier, particularly in food storage and budgeting. She explained that she could now purchase food items in bulk, preserve them in a freezer and reduce the frequency of shopping trips. “Aba Power has really affected my life positively in so many ways. As a mother and a wife, and also as a housekeeper, a house manager, if I may say, it has really helped me because now we have steady light,” she said. While the experiences of residents, manufacturers and institutions point to significant gains, the wider impact will depend on the consistency, affordability and reach of the electricity service. The post Electricity: Geometric Power puts Aba ahead of Nigerian cities appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Mahama tasks Ambassador to Qatar to build on goodwill between Ghana and Qatar
items.description: President John Dramani Mahama has tasked Ghana’s newly appointed Ambassador to Qatar, Mr Louis Kwame Obeng, to build on the goodwill generated between Ghana and Qatar through high-level engagements and direct it towards partnerships that support Ghana’s development priorities. The President said relations between Ghana and Qatar offered considerable opportunities for deeper cooperation in investment, trade, tourism and development. President Mahama gave the charge on Friday when he formally commissioned Mr Obeng and three other newly appointed envoys at the Presidency in Accra. The other envoys are Nana Antwiwaa Dodoo, Ambassador to Angola; Mrs Evelyn Korantemaa Ofosu-Amable, Ambassador to Israel; and Mr Jedidiah Reuben Adogla, Ghana’s Permanent Representative to Geneva, Switzerland. The President urged Mr Obeng to pay particular attention to the effective implementation of the labour mobility agreement between Ghana and Qatar. He stressed that employment opportunities for Ghanaians in Qatar must be accompanied by clear safeguards for their rights, welfare and working conditions. President Mahama tasked the Ambassador to maintain close contact with Ghanaian nationals in Qatar and ensure that any concerns affecting them were promptly raised with the appropriate authorities. He further charged Mr Obeng to advance bilateral cooperation in skills development and employment and sustain engagement on outstanding agreements between the two countries. These include the Joint Committee on Manpower Regulation and the Memorandum of Understanding on Military Cooperation. President Mahama reiterated that the success of Ghana’s bilateral relations must ultimately be measured by the tangible benefits they deliver to citizens. He said the country would measure the value of these relationships by the benefits they deliver to all Ghanaians.

items.title: Persisting fault lines
items.description: HISTORY, it has famously been said, repeats itself first as tragedy and then as farce. Today, it is repeating itself in Pakistan as both tragedy and farce. Recent events have deepened some of the country’s overlapping fault lines — enduring features that have shaped its political landscape for decades. Together they have contributed to its chronic instability and impeded its progress. It has meant the absence of a calm and predictable environment in which to meet the country’s growing challenges. The country seems caught in a time warp with a power elite ensuring it cannot escape its past. Four fault lines (there are others too) are laid bare by recent political developments: unceasing confrontation between the government and opposition; centre-province conflict resulting in dismissal of elected provincial governments; parliament’s marginal role in the political system; and weak institutions whose evolution is stymied or independence eroded by predatory ruling elites. The ongoing confrontation between the PML-N-led government and PTI may have novel aspects but it reflects a long-standing fault line in the country’s divisive politics. Government-opposition conflicts have been endemic in Pakistan’s history, with political behaviour driven by the ethic of war rather than competition. Political leaders and parties have viewed opponents as enemies to be eliminated from the political arena in a terminal conflict, not rivals to compete with, much less accommodated. Branding opponents as disloyal to the country is a well-worn, unseemly tradition. This is evident today by the disingenuous narrative peddled by federal ministers that the ousted KP government was aligned with terrorist organisations. A culture of compromise, tolerance, and restraint never took root leaving ruling and opposition parties perpetually at loggerheads. This, in turn, opened the door to both direct and indirect interventions by the military, which could always count on support from one political party or another to oust governments and expand its power. Divide and rule strategies pursued by the establishment also fuelled political conflict. Some enduring aspects of the political landscape are holding Pakistan back. There were rare moments of political consensus as for example when the 1973 Constitution was adopted, Charter of Democracy agreed (but never implemented) between Benazir Bhutto and Nawaz Sharif in 2006 and in more recent years, the unanimous passage of the 18th Constitutional Amendment in 2010. Beyond these and some other exceptions, the tradition of intolerance and authoritarian behaviour has persisted. Opposition parties have rarely accepted the legitimacy of governments while governments refused to recognise opposition as a legitimate activity fundamental to democracy. The underlying reason has usually been disputed elections. Pakistan’s history is replete with losing sides contesting results and alleging ballot fraud, often for good reason. This happened most recently in the 2024 election which, despite its controversial nature, still saw PTI winning a plurality in the national legislature. It was blocked from forming the federal government by an alliance between its opponents and the establishment. Its uncompromising conduct today stems from what it sees as a stolen election and political manoeuvring to keep it out of power. While linked to government-opposition conflict, the second fault line is distinct: troubled relations and friction between the centre and provinces, which have punctuated the country’s history and weakened federalism. Intolerance of opposition-controlled provincial governments by parties governing at the centre became a common feature from the very inception of Pakistan. Just seven days after independence, the NWFP government was deposed, setting an unfortunate precedent. Thereafter, every province saw elected governments replaced by governor’s rule at some time or another, undermining the federation and testing the country’s unity. The consequences of intolerance of rivals together with the establishment’s efforts to centralise power and failure to make the federal arrangement work, were writ large in the rise of the Bengali nationalist movement that culminated in the break-up of Pakistan in 1971. But no lesson was learnt and the fault line endured. Fast forward to the 1990s when the regionalised nature of election outcomes meant that parties forming governments at the federal level were often different from those that constituted provincial governments. This should have urged efforts to establish smooth and cooperative centre-province relations. But that did not happen. The notion that reciprocal obligations between the centre and provinces are more than a constitutional precept and actually have to be fulfilled by both sides still finds few takers. A third fault line relates to parliament’s weakness and its inability to play its fundamental role of exercising oversight of executive actions and hold governments to account. Successive governments have viewed parliament principally as a means to maintain themselves in power rather than a forum to initiate and debate laws and policy. The preferred mode of legislating has often been through ordinance or using a brute majority to rush through laws without deliberation. This reduced parliament to little more than a rubber stamp. The most recent examples are the 26th and 27th Constitutional amendments that were steamrolled through parliament in 2024 and 2025 without real debate and without even sharing their texts with members before moving them. There was virtually no debate when the two chambers recently endorsed the imposition of emergency in KP. Few if any governments encouraged parliament to play an active legislative and deliberative role. Instead, they preferred the legislature to be a passive body. This remains the case. Even ruling parties with handsome majorities failed to recognise parliament’s utility as a forum to ventilate, change and share opinion. Whether this reflects lack of confidence in their backbenchers or poor understanding of how parliament should function, the outcome is marginalisation of the legislature’s role. This denudes the political system of democratic accountability. The fourth fault line — weak institutions — is no less consequential. It is rooted in a political culture that has privileged personalities over institutions, and in a ruling elite that has little appetite for strong institutions because they impose checks and balances and place limits on power. Nothing illustrates this better than the judiciary. Its independence has been steadily eroded over the years by both civilian and military governments. The recent constitutional amendments have taken this further, making the superior judiciary subservient to the executive. Political fault lines are not cast in stone. Their persistence doesn’t mean they cannot be overcome especially when their impact on the country is so damaging. But it requires bold, visionary leadership to break from the past. The writer is a former ambassador to the US, UK and UN. Published in Dawn, October 19th, 2026

items.title: Gov’t secures €323m to end water crisis in Tamale, Yendi, Damongo
items.description: The government has secured a total of €323 million financing package for the Northern Ghana Water and Sanitation Project to address persistent water shortages in Tamale, Yendi and Damongo. The project is expected to benefit nearly 1.5 million people people, providing safe drinking water, improving sanitation, public health, and supporting climate resilience for the beneficiary communities. Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Baah Forson announced the package on the margins of the 2026 International Monetary Fund (IMF)/World Band Group (WBG) annual meetings in Bangkok. The development emerged from a high-level meeting with European Investment Bank (EIB) Vice-President Ambroise Fayolle, which focused on finalising the terms for the Northern Ghana Water and Sanitation Project. The financing comprise a €225 million highly concessional facility from the EIB, a €68m grant from the European Commission, and a €30m grant from the Dutch government’s Invest International initiative. “I have just concluded a productive meeting with European Investment Bank Vice-President Ambroise Fayolle on the financing package for the Northern Ghana Water and Sanitation Project,” he said. The Finance Minister expressed optimism that the project would address the recurring water shortages and improve sanitation across the three communities in the two Northern regions and the Savannah region. Information provided by the European Investment Bank indicates that the project would improve access to safely managed drinking water services for approximately 1.349m people in the Greater Tamale area. The Bank noted that some 105,000 people in Damongo, covering urban and peri-urban populations were to also benefit from the project. Prior to the project financing conclusion, a baseline water quality assessment exercise was conducted in January 2026 to establish the existing condition of the White Volta River passing through Yapei to its natural source for use. It was observed that the White Volta River exhibited typical freshwater physicochemical characteristics, with neutral pH values ranging from 7.34 to 7.63, low conductivity, and low total dissolved solids, all within applicable national and WHO guideline limits. However, key physical parameters such as turbidity (28.7–30.3 NTU), apparent colour (60–65 Hz), and total suspended solids (28–30 mg/L) exceeded the GS 175:2017 drinking water guideline values at all sampling locations (upstream, intake, and downstream). The baseline study approved the White Volta River as a sustainable source for the project, urging conventional treatment. This includes coagulation, flocculation, sedimentation, filtration, iron removal and disinfection to ensure safe drinking water.

items.title: Covering Nehr-i-Khayyam poses risk of urban flooding: experts
items.description: • Clifton residents, environmentalists stage rally to protest construction at key waterway • Demand suspension of work until EIA is conducted and project details are made public KARACHI: Expressing concern over construction at Nehr-i-Khayyam, an open drain in Clifton’s Block 5, residents and environmentalists from across the city held an awareness walk on Sunday, fearing that covering the drain would reduce its width and pave the way for “commercial activity”. Holding placards with messages such as “Commercial use of Nehr-i-Khayyam not accepted” and “Stop concreting drains, restore Nehr-i-Khayyam”,“Save Nehr-i-Khayyam and stop urban flooding”, the participants gathered near the construction site and said trees had previously been present on both sides of the drain, but now remained on only one side, with just a few left along the stretch where construction was under way. Dawn visited the site and observed that construction was underway on one side of the drain, where two columns had been built. Half of the columns had been plastered with cement, while T-shaped concrete blocks lay nearby. Standing behind a banner bearing the words “Save Nehr-i-Khayyam”, Rasha Tarek, a protester and member of the Karachi Residents’ Community (District South), questioned the practice of discharging sewage into the waterway and then using its pollution to justify covering more than half of it. “Where in the world do people discharge sewage into a waterway, then claim that its water is polluted and proceed to cover over half of it?” she asked. She added that they had stood up for the city and urged everyone to unite to save the waterway. She also demanded an environmental impact assessment (EIA) and said residents should be informed about the project. Masood Lohar, founder and CEO of the Clifton Urban Forest and an environmentalist, claimed that the project had been approved by the Sindh cabinet in 2019 for “recreational purposes”. He alleged that the construction was intended for commercial activity. He said that if an EIA hearing had been held, its details should be made public and the authorities should disclose which civil society representatives or residents had been invited to attend. Expressing concern, he said the authorities were blocking a major intertidal channel between two creeks, adding that the city had already been choked. He termed the matter a “national security issue”. He warned that if Karachi received 250mm of rainfall, the port and important security installations could become dysfunctional. Another environmentalist, Yasir Husain, said he had joined the protest to show solidarity with the community. He added that under the law, every government project should undergo an environmental assessment. He said the purpose of the project remained unclear, as its details had not yet been shared. Mr Husain said that a one-kilometre stretch of the drain, from Ocean Mall to Boat Basin, had suddenly been taken up for construction and a platform had now been built over it. He added he would file a right-to-information request to obtain details of the project. Meanwhile, he added, the protest would continue every weekend. He said he had only been able to obtain information that the project fell under the local government department and was titled “Rehabilitation of Nehr-i-Khayyam, including diversion of sewerage water, district South”. “This project is not about cleaning sewage,” he said, adding that “it is a commercial project, and the sewage will end up in the sea”. Actor Tipu Sharif, who stood alongside other protesters, said he had been a resident of the area for the past 25 years. He claimed that over the past four years, he had witnessed rapid commercialisation in the area. He questioned why the waterway could not be allowed to remain in its original form, asking, “If it was built as a waterway, why not let it remain one? Why is it necessary to cover everything with cement?” He warned that the waterway had helped prevent rainwater from accumulating during heavy rainfall in the area. However, if it was covered, blocked or narrowed, garbage could obstruct the flow of rainwater and create problems during the rainy season. In a press statement, residents of the area demanded the suspension of construction until the required environmental assessment had been conducted and approval obtained from the Sindh Environmental Protection Agency. They also demanded the disclosure of project documents, including the design, and the preservation of the channel’s full original width and banks as open public land. The statement further called for an end to the discharge of untreated sewage into the channel and demanded that wastewater be treated before reaching Boat Basin and the sea. Published in Dawn, October 19th, 2026

items.title: Mahama directs Ambassador to Israel to uphold Ghana’s commitment to two-state solution
items.description: President John Dramani Mahama has directed Ghana’s newly appointed Ambassador to Israel, Mrs Evelyn Korantemaa Ofosu-Amable, to uphold Ghana’s longstanding commitment to a two-state solution to the Palestine-Israel conflict. The President gave the directive on Friday when he commissioned Mrs Ofosu-Amable and three other newly appointed envoys at the Presidency in Accra. The other appointees are Mr Jedidiah Reuben Adogla, Ghana’s Permanent Representative to Geneva, Switzerland; Nana Antwiwaa Dodoo, Ambassador to Angola; and Mr Louis Kwame Obeng, Ambassador to Qatar. President Mahama said in the discharge of her duties, Mrs Ofosu-Amable must remain guided by Ghana’s established foreign policy position on the Palestinian question. “We recognise the sovereign State of Palestine and support a viable two-state solution in which Israel and Palestine will live side by side in peace and security within internationally recognised and secure borders,” the President said. “Our engagement must consistently uphold international law, the protection of civilians, and the dignity of all people.” The President emphasised that the credibility of the international system depended on the consistent application of these principles. President Mahama noted that Ghana’s cooperation with Israel in agriculture, technology, healthcare, water management and education continued to present significant opportunities for national development. He, therefore, urged the Ambassador to identify and promote partnerships that would strengthen Ghanaian expertise and address clearly defined national development needs. The President said an immediate priority for the Mission would be advancing discussions on the proposed labour-mobility agreement between Ghana and Israel. He emphasised that any arrangement involving the deployment of qualified Ghanaian health professionals must adequately protect their rights and welfare while taking into account Ghana’s own healthcare workforce requirements. President Mahama also directed Mrs Ofosu-Amable to maintain regular contact with Ghanaian agricultural interns participating in the MASHAV programme in Israel. He said their safety, welfare, and training conditions required continuous monitoring and active oversight. The President tasked the Ambassador to identify potential concerns at an early stage and take prompt action to address them, drawing lessons from previous experiences involving Ghanaian trainees abroad.

items.title: FG disagrees with World Bank over H1 124% debt servicing/revenue ratio
items.description: By Emma Ujah, Abuja Bureau Chief The Federal Government has disagreed with the World Bank on the latter’s debt servicing/revenue ratio for the first half of 2026, put at 124 percent. The bank in its recent Nigeria Development Update (NDU) reported that federal government debt servicing was 124 percent above its revenue. However, the Federal Ministry of Finance, in a statement, yesterday, faulted the bank’s analysis, explaining that the debt servicing figure included those of the state governments and that it was, therefore, wrong to analyse it against the federal government revenue for the period under consideration. The statement read in part, “This conclusion is misleading, for three reasons, the government said. “The interest figure includes debt the Federal Government services on behalf of other tiers of government, including external loans to states. “Measuring this against federal revenue alone overstates the ratio which is only meaningful when debt and revenue cover the same level of government. “The reported revenue is also incomplete. It excludes independent revenue already earned by government agencies and enterprises but not yet remitted to the Treasury. ” In addition, more revenue is typically earned in the second half of the year than in the first due to the statutory timing of certain tax payments. This is why the ratio stood at 156% in H1 2025, while the full-year 2025 debt-service-to-revenue ratio was below 60%, down from 97% before the reforms. ” This is a clear sign of the progress delivered by the current administration’s reforms. “Between the first half of 2025 and the first half of 2026, federal revenue rose by 72%, from ₦3.6 trillion to ₦6.2 trillion. Interest payments rose by a much slower 38%, from ₦5.6 trillion to ₦7.7 trillion. ” Revenue is therefore growing almost twice as fast as interest costs. As a result, the interest-to-revenue ratio fell by 32 percentage points in a single year, from 156% to 124%, and the gap between interest and revenue narrowed from ₦2.0 trillion to ₦1.5 trillion. This is the result of reforms working, not a sign of fiscal distress. “Debt sustainability is assessed on a full-year basis, not over six months. The same World Bank report projects Nigeria’s full-year 2026 debt service, covering both interest and principal, at 46% of revenue. “This is the appropriate benchmark, and a guide to avoid the invalid conclusions being drawn. “Every naira borrowed by the Federal Government falls within the limits approved by the National Assembly under the 2026 Appropriation Act and the approved borrowing plan. “All borrowing is conducted in full compliance with the Fiscal Responsibility Act 2007 and the Debt Management Office (Establishment) Act 2003, and is published regularly by the Debt Management Office. “The Ministry welcomes informed scrutiny of public finances. We encourage analysts and commentators to apply the same rigour they seek to hold the government to: compare like with like, read figures in context, and seek clarification where the data is unclear.” The post FG disagrees with World Bank over H1 124% debt servicing/revenue ratio appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: FG turns to bonds to tackle N6trn debt
items.description: With the Federal Government’s debts to power generation companies hitting the N6 trillion mark at the end of 2025, the government has gone to the bond market to raise funds to make up for its inability to fund electricity subsidies from the national budget. NERC, in its 2025 industry report, put the Federal Government’s gross tariff subsidy obligation at N1.928 trillion for the year, representing 57.44 percent of the total NBET invoice. The amount translates to an average subsidy obligation of N160.69 billion per month. The government’s subsidy obligation was distributed across the four quarters, with N536.40 billion recorded in the first quarter, N514.36 billion in the second quarter, N458.76 billion in the third quarter and N418.79 billion in the fourth quarter. The 2025 figure represented a slight decline from the N1.949 trillion subsidy obligation recorded in 2024. The government had in September 2026 signed the N728.979 billion Series 2 bond under its N4 trillion Power Sector Debt Reduction Programme, in a fresh move to settle verified legacy debts owed to electricity generation companies and restore liquidity to Nigeria’s power sector. The transaction comprised N402 billion in cash bonds raised from the domestic capital market and N326.979 billion in non-cash bonds allotted to participating generation companies. The Managing Director/CEO, Nigerian Bulk Electricity Trading Plc, Akin Odeyemi said, at the backdrop of weak growth in power supply the GenCos appear to be shackled by indebtedness by the Federal Government with outstanding debt put around N6 trillion at the beginning of this year. Consequently, the government had in September 2026 signed the N728.979 billion Series 2 bond under its N4 trillion Power Sector Debt Reduction Programme, in a fresh move to settle verified legacy debts owed to electricity generation companies and restore liquidity to Nigeria’s power sector. The transaction comprised N402 billion in cash bonds raised from the domestic capital market and N326.979 billion in non-cash bonds allotted to participating generation companies. Odeyemi said at the weekend that NBET has commenced the settlement of participating Generation Companies (GenCos) and their associated Gas Companies following the successful issuance and signing of the N728.979 billion Series 2 Bonds under the N4 trillion Power Sector Multi-Instrument Issuance Programme. He noted that the milestone “represents a significant step in the implementation of the Presidential Power Sector Debt Reduction Programme, under the visionary leadership of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, and in furtherance of the objectives of the Renewed Hope Agenda. “The settlement is being undertaken through a combination of N402,000,000,000.00 in Cash Bonds and N326,979,000,000.00 in Non-Cash Bonds, in accordance with the approved settlement framework”, he added. Power supply has improved, Power Minister insists Despite concerns over the sector’s performance, the Minister of Power, Mr. Joseph Tegbe, has insisted that electricity supply has improved over the past three months. Tegbe, who acknowledged that some parts of the country continued to experience poor supply, said the government was working to address the challenges. According to him, “Operational record reports show generation and transmission above 5,000MW over the past couple of weeks, compared to the 3,700 to 4,700MW range before June, and a generation peak of 5,330MW during August and September. “Our next task is to sustain these gains and translate them into more dependable supply at customer level. We are aware that a national peak alone cannot describe the experience of every community.” He said the government’s efforts to address the challenges were anchored on three pillars: stabilising the value chain, restoring market discipline and strengthening governance. “Under the first pillar, the 375MW Alaoji open-cycle power plant was restored to the national grid after three years offline. “A number of substations have been upgraded. For instance, new transformers have been commissioned at Apapa, Ijora, Alausa and Lekki in Lagos, unlocking 672MW of transmission capacity, while a new 300MVA transformer has been energised at Katampe in Abuja, unlocking another 240MW of transmission capacity. “These interventions restored existing assets and strengthened the network serving major centres of demand.” The Minister said the government was also working to diversify the country’s energy mix, with emphasis on solar power. He said the completed electrification portfolio under the REA and its partners comprised 62 solar and mini-grid installations across 30 states, representing about 43.6MW of installed solar capacity and 41,735 new connections, with an estimated reach of more than 208,000 people. Reform remains unfinished —Babalola Speaking on the state of the power sector, Special Adviser to the President on Power and Chairman, Presidential Task Force on Power Sector Reset and Restoration, Dr. Lanre Babalola, said the reforms initiated by the government remained incomplete. Babalola noted that Nigeria’s electricity challenge was not simply a lack of generation capacity. “Our deeper problem is that we have not yet built a system capable of consistently converting available capacity into reliable electricity, commercial value and sustainable investment,” he said. According to him, “We must also recognise that Nigeria’s electricity reform remains an unfinished transition. “We unbundled the old vertically integrated utility. Generation and distribution assets were privatised. A bulk trader was established. And we expected private capital and commercial discipline to progressively transform the industry. “But we never fully completed the transition to the competitive electricity market envisaged by those reforms. “The single-buyer model was conceived as a transitional mechanism. NBET provided a credible intermediary while market participants developed the creditworthiness required for direct contracting. “But a transitional mechanism becomes a structural constraint if the transition never happens. The objective cannot be to preserve the institutions of transition indefinitely. The objective must be to complete the transition.” Nigerians have been paying for darkness’ — Fadipe Reacting to the figures, lawyer and Lead Consultant at Sage Consulting on Power Sector, Mr. Bode Fadipe, said the data raised questions about whether consumers had received commensurate value for the money paid for electricity. “What this data has just confirmed is that Nigerians have been paying for darkness,” Fadipe said. He identified inadequate investment as one of the major challenges responsible for the limited improvement in electricity supply, arguing that the figures also justified NERC’s directive requiring DisCos to retain part of their revenue for investment. “You will recall that the DisCos vehemently protested this order, but NERC thankfully insisted on the implementation of the order,” he said. Fadipe, however, said the level of compliance with the investment directive remained a separate issue that needed to be established. He called for closer monitoring of DisCos and strict enforcement of NERC’s investment directives. “NERC must dutifully enforce its order on investment. NERC must also set timelines for certain levels of improvement,” he said. He further advocated forensic audits of investments by DisCos to determine whether funds earmarked for infrastructure were being properly utilised, while urging NERC to work with market participants on debt recovery. Consumers demand stronger protection Also reacting, consumer rights advocate and Executive Director, Electricity Consumer Protection Advocacy Centre, Chief Princewill Okorie, said the revenue figures raised questions about the quality of service delivered to consumers. Okorie said the decentralisation of the electricity sector under the new legal framework had brought regulation closer to consumers in the states, but argued that enforcement of consumer protection provisions remained a major challenge. According to him, consumers continued to face issues including estimated billing, infrastructure charges and alleged non-compliance with regulatory directives. He alleged that in some communities, consumers had been compelled to contribute money for transformers and other distribution infrastructure despite regulatory obligations on DisCos. “Consumers are not paying” has often been cited as a reason for poor service, Okorie said, but argued that the quality and basis of bills issued to consumers must also be examined. “The appropriate question to ask is: how did they generate these bills? Were they justifiably, accountably and transparently generated?” he said. He called for stronger enforcement of electricity regulations and greater protection for consumers, particularly in rural communities. Okorie also advocated a dedicated mechanism for investigating alleged electricity-related violations and improving consumer awareness of their rights. He questioned why the Federal Ministry of Power did not have a dedicated consumer protection unit and urged stronger involvement by consumer protection authorities in educating electricity users about their rights. He also questioned claims that the Federal Government was paying subsidies in the sector, noting that electricity consumers provide much of the equipment used by DisCos, including poles, cables and transformers, without reimbursement from the utilities. items.title: 2027: I won’t step down for ADC, Kwankwaso declares
items.description: …says party no better than APC By Luminous Jannamike ABUJA – Senator Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso, vice-presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC, has ruled out withdrawing from the 2027 presidential race in favour of the African Democratic Congress, ADC, declaring that the opposition party offers no better alternative to the ruling All Progressives Congress, APC. Kwankwaso’s declaration comes amid opposition manoeuvres ahead of the election, with the NDC chieftain accusing the ADC Presidential Campaign Council, PCC, of promoting claims that his ticket with Peter Obi is working for the APC or may step down for the ADC candidate at the last minute. In a statement on Sunday, Kwankwaso accused the ADC campaign team of directing unnecessary attacks at him, Obi and the NDC instead of selling its own candidate to Nigerians. “We will not withdraw our candidature for the ADC or any other party,” he declared. Kwankwaso also dismissed suggestions that the NDC ticket was acting on behalf of the ruling party, insisting that it remained committed to contesting the election. “The OK ticket is neither working for nor acting on behalf of the APC or any of its candidates. We see no possibility or reason to withdraw from the presidential race in favour of the ADC candidate or any other,” he said. Turning his attention to the ADC campaign council, Kwankwaso urged it to address allegations levelled against its presidential candidate by Vice-President Kashim Shettima rather than attack the NDC ticket. He also rejected the ADC’s claim to being an alternative to the APC-led government, which he accused of failing Nigerians. “The APC-led government has failed Nigerians. The ADC offers no better alternative,” Kwankwaso declared. Presenting the NDC as a stronger opposition platform, he said his ticket with Obi had the credibility, capacity and nationwide support to unite the country and tackle insecurity, education, agriculture, infrastructure, healthcare and economic challenges. Kwankwaso urged supporters and well-meaning Nigerians to remain committed to the party’s electoral victory, describing the NDC as the country’s most formidable opposition party. “I therefore urge all our supporters and well-meaning Nigerians to continue working toward the victory of our great party,” he said. The post 2027: I won’t step down for ADC, Kwankwaso declares appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Presidency, Makinde at ‘war’ over N250bn NLNG dividend
items.description: By Johnbosco Agbakwuru & Adeola Badru ABUJA — THE Presidency yesterday described as false Oyo State governor, Seyi Makinde’s latest claim that the federal government was withholding N250 billion in NLNG dividend windfall for each state of the federation, asking that it be disregarded. Read Also: DisCos’ revenue rises 450% as debt profile hits N700bn It also noted that, going by Governor Makinde’s claim, a one-off distribution of N250 billion to each of the 36 states would amount to N9 trillion, excluding the federal government, FCT and the 774 local councils, adding that NLNG had never paid $25 billion in dividends to the Federation Account in a single payout. The governor, who is also the presidential candidate of Allied Peoples Movement, APM, had alleged that the federal government was withholding the amount meant for states until the 2027 elections were over. But in a statement issued yesterday by the Special Adviser to the President on Information and Strategy, Bayo Onanuga, the Presidency said any claim that a single payout exceeded the company’s entire lifetime distribution to the federation, and was being withheld, defied basic logic and economic reality. Tinubu running voodoo economy However, the governor, through the Makinde-Daura Campaign Organisation, double-down on his allegation last night, dismissing the Presidency’s denial and insisting the President was running a voodoo economy. Makinde’s claim false — Presidency The Presidency’s statement read: “The Presidency wishes to clarify Governor Seyi Makinde’s claim that the federal government is withholding N250 billion in NLNG dividends for each state of the federation. “At the 2027 Budget Stakeholders’ Consultative Engagement held at the Olola Ogunlana Hall, International Conference Centre, University of Ibadan, on Friday, Makinde claimed the funds would not be released until after the 2027 elections. He further claimed that the federal government had spent the money. “‘Each state was supposed to get N250 billion. We had already identified projects that would expand Oyo State’s economy. But they have now said the money will not be paid until after the election. Is the election more important than the people of Nigeria?’ the governor further said. The Presidency said ‘Makinde’s latest claim that the federal government is withholding the NLNG dividend windfall is false and should be disregarded.’ “Giving details on the subject matter, the Presidency said: ‘Here are the facts the public should know about how the Federation Account is managed and how money is shared among the three tiers of government. Even as a one-off distribution, N250 billion to each of the 36 states amounts to N9.0 trillion, excluding the Federal Government, the FCT and the 774 local councils. “Under the Federation Account Allocation Committee, FAAC, formula, states receive 26.72 per cent of the distributable Federation Account revenue. For the states’ share alone to reach N9 trillion, total NLNG dividends paid into the Federation Account would have to exceed N33.68 trillion, about $25 billion, in a single declaration. NLNG has never paid $25bn in dividends “NLNG has never paid $25 billion in dividends to the Federation Account in a single payout. NLNG has paid approximately $21.5 billion in dividends to the Federation over the last 25 years, with less than $3 billion realised since President Bola Ahmed Tinubu assumed office. “Therefore, any claim that a single payout exceeds the company’s entire lifetime distribution to the Federation, and is being withheld, defies basic logic and economic reality. “We expect Governor Makinde to be more measured in his public conduct and utterances. Since he embarked on his presidential bid, he has chosen to play politics by making misleading claims rather than presenting verifiable facts. Indeed, he has turned false, unguarded statements and claims into an art form. “‘He once described the huge financial flow from the Federation Account to states, including Oyo, as ‘voodoo’. It stated that under Nigerian law, Governor Makinde is free to pursue his presidential ambition. ‘’He should desist from making falsehoods and disinformation the hallmarks of his campaign. We urge the public to disregard these unfounded claims, which serve only to mislead citizens and stoke needless disaffection against the federal authorities.’’ Makinde to FG: Explain N9trn NLNG dividends shortfall to states Doubling-down on the allegation last night, Governor Makinde challenged the Presidency to explain how dividends paid by NLNG into the Federation Account were distributed, insisting that a reconciliation exercise identified an alleged shortfall of about N9 trillion due to states and local governments. Makinde in a statement signed by his Special Adviser on Media, Dr Sulaimon Olanrewaju, accused the Presidency of sidestepping the central issue, which it said was a reconciliation exercise conducted by a consultant engaged by the Nigeria Governors’ Forum, NGF, with the support of the federal government, to establish the status of NLNG dividend payments. He said the exercise identified a shortfall of about N9 trillion owed to states and local governments, adding that the federal government had accepted the findings. “The report remains in the custody of both the federal government and the NGF. We trust the Presidency will not deny its existence,” the statement said. The governor’s aide also noted that Makinde was the incumbent vice-chairman of the NGF, a position it cited in defending the basis of his claim. He further questioned the Presidency’s assertion that NLNG had paid $21.5 billion in dividends into the Federation Account since the company began operations, including $3 billion received under the current administration. While acknowledging that the Presidency had provided those figures, the governor’s media aide said it had failed to explain how the funds were distributed among the beneficiaries. “But it did not explain how these funds were disbursed. Have states and local governments received their shares? How much did they receive? And how were those amounts calculated? What happened to the $3 billion received under this administration?” he queried. The governor’s aide maintained that the questions were central to the dispute over the alleged withholding of the dividends and called on the Presidency to provide details of the payments and their distribution. Defending Makinde’s position, the aide said the governor was not given to making claims without supporting evidence. “Governor Makinde conducts public discourse with decorum and does not make unfounded claims or quote figures without a basis,” he said. He also reaffirmed the governor’s readiness to provide further information on the matter, while urging the Presidency to address the substance of the allegations rather than sidestepping the issues raised. “We remain ready to provide further clarification while we urge the Presidency to address the substance of the matter,” he added. Makinde-Daura Campaign dismisses Presidency’s denial Also dismissing the Presidency’s denial last night, the Makinde-Daura Campaign Organisation, in a statement signed by Director of Communications, Richard Nnanna Ihediwa, said: ‘’The attention of the Makinde-Daura Presidential Campaign Organization, MDPCO, has been drawn to the lame attempt by the Tinubu Presidency to evade the core issues raised by the presidential candidate of the APM and governor of Oyo State, Seyi Makinde, that the Nigeria Liquefied Natural Gas dividend accruable to states is being withheld by the Tinubu-led federal government. “Instead of coming clean on why the fund is withheld, the Tinubu Presidency, in its characteristic resort to lies, falsehood, distortions and propaganda left the issue to play around with unsupported figures in the bid to hoodwink Nigerians and divert public attention from this constitutional violation and assault on the states “If the Tinubu Presidency claims that Engr Makinde is wrong in his assertion that N250 billion NLNG dividend meant for states is being withheld, we challenge President Tinubu to directly tell Nigerians if the said dividends have been paid to the states, rather than resorting to personal attacks on the APM presidential candidate. “The Presidency appears carried away by its own display of imperial grandeur, forgetting that Nigeria remains a democracy in which demanding accountability for public funds is a civic right, not an offence. Governor Makinde’s presidential ambition does not in any way deny him that right, nor does it exempt the federal government from legitimate scrutiny. “Moreover, and importantly so, does the Presidency has any constitutional powers to withhold any funds accruing to the states in a Federation? “We, therefore, challenge the Presidency to publish the relevant NLNG dividend receipts, Federation Account Allocation Committee, FAAC, decisions and official communications establishing the amounts received, the sums approved for distribution and the timing of the proposed payments to states. “Nigerians deserve clear answers to three fundamental questions of how much the NLNG pay in dividends during the period under discussion and the amount credited to the Federation Account. They need to know how much was approved for distribution to the states. “Invoking NLNG’s cumulative dividend payments in the last 25 years does not answer these questions. Historical totals cannot, by themselves, establish the amount received during a specific period and the sum available for distribution. It does not answer whether a particular payment was proposed, approved, received, delayed or withheld. Those questions can only be settled by the relevant financial records. “If the Presidency’s argument is that allocating N250 billion to each of the 36 states would amount to N9 trillion, a sum NLNG has never paid as a single dividend as it alleged, that calculation does not resolve the matter. “The question is not whether N9 trillion was ever paid in a single transaction, but the amount that is actually under discussion as can be established by the official records. “Engr. Makinde, the governor of Oyo State and Presidential candidate of the APM is known for his integrity. He is not given to propaganda and disinformation which are the known stock-in-trade and policy direction of the Tinubu-led All Progressives Congress, APC, administration. “He has maintained a clean, issue-based campaign devoid of mudslinging, misinformation, disinformation and propaganda for which the APC is known. “The MDPCO stands by Engr. Makinde in his assertion that President Tinubu is running a voodoo economy where government thrive on lies, where the national fortunes only improve on papers with no corresponding improvement in the harsh everyday life of citizens under his administration. “In any event, our campaign is aware that President Tinubu and his APC have been jittery and restless over Engr. Makinde’s soaring popularity and the widespread acceptance of his RESET NIGERIA Agenda message across the nation since the commencement of the campaign. “The Tinubu Presidency is disturbed because Nigerians have identified Engr. Makinde as a credible alternative to President Tinubu, leading to the massive surge to his campaign and the APM. It should therefore come to terms with the fact that no amount of propaganda and lies against Engr. Makinde will help President Tinubu at this time.’’ Vanguard News The post Presidency, Makinde at ‘war’ over N250bn NLNG dividend appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Thousands fill Accra Sports Stadium for Shattafest 2026
items.description: Ghanaian dancehall artiste Shatta Wale delivered an energetic and emotional performance at the Accra Sports Stadium as thousands of fans gathered for Shattafest 2026, which coincided with his birthday celebration. The musician broke down in tears while looking across the packed stadium during his performance, in one of the memorable moments of the night. Shatta Wale, dressed in white, stepped onto the stage in gigantic fashion to a rousing welcome from thousands of his fans. He performed several of his street bangers for hours with members of his Shatta Movement fanbase and other music enthusiasts adoring his stagecraft. Several Ghanaian artistes, including Medikal, Fancy Gadam, Sista Afia, Edem and Patapaa, also appeared at the event to support Shatta Wale. The 2026 festival was organised in partnership with MobileMoney Fintech Limited (MMFL), building on the collaboration between the company and the musician during Shattafest 2025 at Independence Square in Accra. The partnership combines entertainment with customer engagement and efforts to promote the adoption of digital financial services. Shatta Wale had also expressed a desire to develop the festival into an annual celebration and eventually extend it to other parts of Ghana and beyond. This year’s music festival would go down as a massive success and one of the biggest concerts of the year, despite Shatta Wale making some controversial statements on stage. The 2026 event also received support from corporate partners, including Ecobank, Guinness Ghana, AT, Shaxi and Waya among the sponsors.

items.title: LITERARY NOTES: Despite criticism, Hayaat-i-Javed and Sir Syed live on
items.description: EVEN 128 years after his death, Sir Syed Ahmed Khan lives on. Born on Oct 17, 1817, Sir Syed passed away in 1898, but he has been endowed with Hayaat-i-Javed, or the eternal life, it seems. True to its name, Hayaat-i-Javed (1901), Sir Syed’s biography penned by Altaf Husain Hali, too, along with Sir Syed, has lived for over 125 years. Though Hayaat-i-Javed was received well, both Sir Syed and his biography could not escape scathing remarks from doubters. Shibli No’mani’s sardonic comments, criticising Hayaat-i-Javed , have become almost proverbial and today one can hardly read or review the book without recalling Shibli, who said it was ‘kitaab-ul-manaaqib’ (book of virtues) and ‘ mudallal maddahi’ (eulogy supported by reasoning). Despite the criticism, the book is considered a milestone when it comes to biography writing in Urdu and is very much a part of Urdu’s literary canon because of its impact and lasting value. But in many of the review articles on Hayaat-i-Javed an objective and research-based approach to see its actual intent and real literary value was missing, says Dr Shams Badauni, a veteran Indian scholar. To address this lacuna, he has published a book that collects some rare and contemporaneous reviews on Hayaat-i-Javed , along with some not-so-old ones. But his book is not just another run-of-the-mill job that puts together a few articles, pasted with a limping, half-cooked intro, as is the norm. Rather, Mutal’a-iHayaat-i-Javed Ke Aik Sau Pachchees Saal, or 125 years of the study of Hayaat-i-Javed, is an editing work that can teach a few lessons to the young researchers on how to compile and edit literary works, using the principles of textual criticism. In addition to his research-based annotations, Badauni has written two prefaces and both are research papers unto themselves, sifting through the heaps of the material on Hali, Sir Syed and Hayaat-i-Javed. Dr Badauni thinks Hayaat-i-Javed also serves as an intellectual history of the 19th-century Muslims in the subcontinent, as well as Sir Syed’s life and his achievements. He says its study is in fact a study of the history of evolution of Muslim thought in the subcontinent. Badauni’s first preface discusses Hayaat-i-Javed in detail, chronicling how and when it was written and published. It describes the earlier attempts at writing Sir Syed’s biography and says his first biography was written by G. F. I. Graham (1840-1928) in English, published in 1885. Qazi Sirajuddin Ahmed (1867-1925), a scholar from Rawalpindi and editor of Chaudhveen Sadi, had finished writing Sir Syed’s first-ever biography in Urdu in 1892, but it remained unpublished. Badauni’s second preface discovers the nature of the association and collaboration between Sir Syed and Hali, something that has hardly been touched by Hali and the readers going through his 900-plus-page book remain unaware of how and when Sir Syed and Hali met for the first time, nor has Hali said anything about what inspired him to join Sir Syed’s historic Aligarh Movement. This preface provides the readers with relevant details, which is quite rare info. Giving the printing history, Badauni says Hayaat-i-Javed , first published in April 1901, is divided into two parts and the second part is meandering, bloated and repetitive, not as organised as the first one. The first part, having 320 pages, covers biographical details in little over 300 pages. The second part had 558 pages and indices took another 100 pages or so, but indices and a few subheadings were axed from the second edition (1903). The earliest reviews on Hayaat-i-Javed were penned by Moulvi Abdul Haq, Abdul Haleem Sharar, Waheeduddin Saleem, Zakaullah and Sir Abdul Qadir and were positive, Abul Kalam Azad showed a few reservations in his review though. The editor and contributors of Oudh Punch, a humour magazine from Lucknow, were already lampooning Sir Syed and they found new material in the shape of Hayaat-i-Javed to satirise both Hali and Sir Syed. Habibur Rahman Shervani in his article said Sir Syed was not qualified to write tafseer, nor was Hali when reviewing it. What aggrieved Hali was not the negative reviews, but the cold reception from Aligarh, which was, perhaps, intended to avoid further controversies on religious issues that had sparked during Sir Syed’s life. Shams Badauni dug up all these rare, century-old pieces and included them in the book. He has included some other important articles on Hayaat-i-Javed by distinguished critics as well as some additional writings that help fully understand the book and its scope. The book, published in September 2026 by Delhi’s Arshiya Publications, has been reprinted by Lahore’s World View Publishers. Published in Dawn, October 19th, 2026

items.title: Global South must work towards better multilateralism – Opoku-Agyemang
items.description: Vice President Professor Jane Naana Opoku-Agyemang, has called for the need for Global South to work towards better multilateralism, with fairer global financial arrangements, stronger representation in international institutions, and greater participation in shaping decisions that affect our countries. “Cooperation does not require us to think alike. We must have the confidence to disagree respectfully, learn from one another’s successes and failures, and continue working together towards shared goals,” she stated. A statement issued by the Office of the Vice President said she made the remarks in Shanghai, China, in her address at the 2026 Global South Academic Forum, convened on the theme “Global South Political Parties: Governance and Modernisation.” At the opening, the Vice President reflected on the historical struggles that shaped the Global South, particularly the pursuit of political independence and the right of nations to determine their own futures. She noted that from the Pan-African vision of Osagyefo Dr Kwame Nkrumah to liberation movements across Asia, Africa, Latin America and the Caribbean, their shared history reminds them that political independence is only the beginning. “The greater task is to build strong institutions, productive economies and systems that respond to our people’s aspirations,” Vice President Opoku-Agyemang stated. “Similarly, winning political power and governing effectively are related but not the same responsibility.” She said political parties, governments, universities, and other institutions must continually evolve, strengthen accountability, and build the capacity to respond to changing realities. She said China’s development experience offers valuable lessons in long-term planning, industrialisation, and institutional coordination. Vice President Opoku-Agyemang said at the same time, meaningful South-South cooperation must be grounded in mutual learning rather than the assumption that countries must follow identical development paths. “Our different histories and circumstances require solutions that reflect our realities.” She also highlighted the importance of strengthening cooperation across research, education, technology, and innovation. The Vice President said as artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies reshape our economies, universities and research institutions across the Global South must collaborate more directly, share knowledge, and develop solutions that meet our societies’ needs. She reiterated that they also need a more representative and equitable international order. She encouraged the Forum to sustain intellectual partnerships, and honest exchanges needed to move beyond familiar debates and towards practical solutions.

items.title: Two moments of madness cost Sri Lanka as Pakistan win tri-series opener after Salman Ali Agha century
items.description: Sri Lanka were cruising. Only 53 runs stood between them and a flying start in the One-day International tri-series opener against Pakistan after Pavan Rathnayake and Janith Liyanage’s 119-run stand. The dew that made the Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium outfield relentlessly slick on Sunday night had also deprived Pakistan’s pacers of the chance to extract reverse swing from the old ball. Then came two moments of madness. Liyanage, who had looked composed throughout his innings, chipped Haris Rauf casually to Babar Azam at long-on before Dasun Shanaka, who had threatened to take the game away from Pakistan, heaved Shaheen Shah Afridi to the same fielder in the same position. In the space of four balls, Sri Lanka unravelled. Naseem Shah then had Sachindu Colombage caught behind, Eshan Malinga was run out after a mix-up, and Haris cleaned up Asitha Fernando to seal a 37-run win for Pakistan, who had earlier posted 305 thanks to Salman Ali Agha’s fourth ODI century. Salman celebrated his return to the Pakistan side after his unceremonious axing from the Test team two months ago with a composed 107 off 90 balls, including 10 fours and a six. Pakistan’s innings, however, finished with a flourish from Sri Lanka’s bowlers, who conceded only 36 runs while taking five wickets in the last five overs. Eshan Malinga led the charge with figures of 4-46. After openers Fakhar Zaman and Saim Ayub fell to Dilshan Madushanka, Babar Azam and Saad Baig steadied the innings with a 74-run partnership for the third wicket. Malinga broke through by bouncing out Babar for 45 and Saad for 39, bringing Salman and Hasan Nawaz together. The pair added 97, with Salman gradually increasing the tempo after initially settling in. He brought up his half-century in the 35th over, rotating the strike and punishing loose deliveries. Salman Agha plays a shot during the tri-series one-day international (ODI) cricket match between Pakistan and Sri Lanka at the Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium in Rawalpindi on October 18, 2026. — AFP Hasan supplied the acceleration with two sixes off Sachindu Colombage, including a powerful slog sweep over cow corner. Salman then took charge, pulling Dasun Shanaka through the leg side before launching Malinga’s slower delivery over long-off for six. He reached three figures in the 45th over, finding the boundary through deep midwicket before edging a full delivery past the infield to third man. Hasan fell for 37, caught by Pavan Rathnayake at short midwicket off Asitha Fernando, who also removed Arafat Minhas for 18. Salman departed for 107 at 279-6, mistiming a lofted shot to Shanaka at long-on, and Sri Lanka seized control. Malinga dismissed Faheem Ashraf and trapped Naseem Shah lbw in the next over, while accurate yorkers restricted Pakistan’s lower order. Haris was run out for a duck in the final over, leaving Pakistan all out for 305 in 49.5 overs. Sri Lanka’s reply began poorly. Shaheen and Naseem made early inroads, reducing the visitors to 91-4 and leaving the chase in need of repair. But as the ball and outfield grew wetter, Pakistan’s bowlers struggled to make the ball grip, allowing Rathnayake and Liyanage to rebuild with patience and calculated aggression. Rathnayake initially played watchfully before cutting Arafat Minhas late through deep point and pulling Saim Ayub to the deep midwicket boundary. He raised his maiden ODI half-century with a single off Arafat in the 31st over, then pulled two short balls from Shaheen over square leg in successive deliveries. Liyanage offered stability at the other end, rotating the strike and punishing anything loose. He drove Naseem through the gap between mid-off and extra cover before dancing down the track to hammer Arafat straight down the ground. Their running between the wickets kept the scoreboard moving as Pakistan struggled to find a breakthrough. Faheem Ashraf (R) bowls as Sri Lanka’s Dasun Shanaka watches during the tri-series one-day international (ODI) cricket match between Pakistan and Sri Lanka at the Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium in Rawalpindi on October 18, 2026. — AFP Faheem finally ended the partnership in the 38th over, when Rathnayake, having faced 74 deliveries, pushed a length ball straight to Salman at short cover. But the wicket did little to ease Pakistan’s anxiety. Shanaka attacked immediately, pulling Faheem for four and driving through extra cover before launching Arafat over square leg for six. Liyanage brought up his half-century with a fierce drive down the ground, and Sri Lanka remained firmly in the contest. With 82 needed from the final 10 overs, the visitors had a genuine chance of pulling off the chase. Then Liyanage’s loose chip and Shanaka’s reckless heave turned a promising pursuit into a collapse. From there, Pakistan needed only to keep their nerve. Salman’s century had given Pakistan the platform; Malinga’s late burst had kept the total within reach. But Sri Lanka’s two costly shots ultimately decided the opener, handing Pakistan a winning start to the tri-series.

items.title: DisCos’ revenue rises 450% as debt profile hits N700bn
items.description: Supply grows by 4.8% Available plant capacity falls by 41% 13 years of privatisation yield little results FG turns to bonds to tackle N6trn debt Power supply has improved, Power Minister insists Consumers, experts react Revenue collected by Nigeria’s electricity Distribution Companies (DisCos) rose by about 450 per cent in eight years, from N218.16 billion in the first half of 2018 to N1.2 trillion in the corresponding period of 2026, far outpacing growth in electricity supply over the period. Data from the Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission (NERC), analysed by Financial Vanguard, showed that while DisCos’ revenue increased by about N983.04 billion, total electricity supply grew by only 4.8 per cent, from 16,861 gigawatt-hours (GWh) in the first half of 2018 to 17,668GWh in the first half of 2026, even as their debt profile in the last six months hits N700billion. The data also indicated that average available generation capacity declined by 41 per cent, from 7,565.5 megawatts (MW) in the first half of 2018 to 4,456MW in the corresponding period of 2026. On an annual basis, DisCos’ revenue increased by about 666 per cent in ten years, from N302.93 billion in 2016 to N2.32 trillion in 2025, highlighting the widening gap between revenue growth and improvements in electricity supply. NERC data showed that while DisCos’ annual revenue rose by about N2.016 trillion over the period, average daily power generation increased by approximately 36 per cent, from 3,276MW in 2016 to 4,475MW in 2025. The disparity has raised concerns about the extent to which increased revenue collections have translated into improved electricity supply and service delivery to consumers, 13 years after the privatisation of the power sector. In the same vein, data from NERC showed that in the first half of 2026, DisCos failed to collect N700.53 billion. It indicated that while the utilities received N1.9trillion worth of energy from the market, they collected N1.2trillion from consumers, leaving a balance of N700 billion. The Rural Electrification Agency (REA) has estimated that about 85 million Nigerians still lack access to electricity. In 2016, DisCos collected N302.925 billion, while total annual electricity supply stood at 23,742GWh. By 2025, revenue had risen by about 666 per cent to N2.3188 trillion, while annual electricity supply increased by 31.6 per cent to 31,251GWh. DisCos’ revenue rose to N370.456 billion in 2017, before increasing to N448.749 billion in 2019 and N542.729 billion in 2020. Collections further climbed to N775.336 billion in 2021 and N841.811 billion in 2022. The upward trend accelerated in subsequent years, with revenue reaching N1.0775 trillion in 2023, N1.6597 trillion in 2024 and N2.3188 trillion in 2025. By comparison, annual electricity supply increased from 23,742GWh in 2016 to 33,489.17GWh in 2019 and 35,242.17GWh in 2020. It rose further to 36,710.60GWh in 2023 and peaked at 37,093.70GWh in 2024 before declining to 31,251GWh in 2025. The divergence was particularly evident in 2025, when annual electricity supply fell by about 15.7 per cent from 37,093.70GWh in 2024, even as DisCos’ revenue increased from N1.6597 trillion to N2.3188 trillion. 13 years of privatisation yield little results The bulk of the power sector was privatised in November 2013, with generation plants and 11 distribution companies handed over to private investors, while the Federal Government retained control of the transmission segment. The arrangement formed the basis of the Nigerian Electricity Supply Industry, NESI. However, 13 years after privatisation, concerns remain over the pace of growth in electricity supply despite over N10 trillion public investment in the sector. NERC data showed that in 2016, three years after privatisation, the average available generation capacity of 27 power plants was 7,527MW, while actual average generation stood at 3,276MW. By 2025, with installed generation capacity of more than 13,000MW, average available capacity had fallen by 28.3 per cent to 5,398MW, while average generation rose to 4,475MW. The post DisCos’ revenue rises 450% as debt profile hits N700bn appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Bekwai MP donates 100 bags of cement, GH¢5,000 to Ankaase palace project
items.description: The Member of Parliament for Bekwai, Ralph Poku-Adusei, has donated 100 bags of cement and GH¢5,000 towards the construction of an ultramodern palace at Ankaase in the Ashanti Region. The contribution was made through his office during celebrations marking the 30th anniversary of the enstoolment of Nana Adomako-Ansa I as Ankaasehene and Kontihene of the Amoafo Traditional Area. The event also marked the fifth anniversary of the enstoolment of the area’s Queen Mother and brought together traditional leaders, community members, teachers, students and other guests. In a goodwill message, Mr Poku-Adusei described Nana Adomako-Ansa I as a fatherly and principled leader whose three decades of traditional leadership had contributed to Ankaase’s development. He recalled first meeting the chief when he served as a registrar at the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST), during the MP’s undergraduate years. He commended the chief’s contribution to improvements in electricity supply, water provision, educational infrastructure, town planning and community facilities. The lawmaker also highlighted the establishment of a Junior High School and a computer laboratory, noting that he was proud to have supported the completion of the laboratory. Mr Poku-Adusei said his contribution to the palace project was intended to support Nana Adomako-Ansa I’s vision of leaving a lasting legacy for the people of Ankaase. He called on traditional leaders to continue supporting and collaborating with him as he pursues his vision of making the Bekwai Constituency self-sufficient. The MP congratulated Nana Adomako-Ansa I and the Queen Mother on their respective anniversaries, recognising their contributions to traditional leadership and community development.
