items.title: Au-delà de la France, la crise du coût de la vie embrase l’Europe
items.description: Des centaines de milliers de personnes ont manifesté ce week-end dans plusieurs pays européens, dont la France, la Belgique, l’Italie, le Portugal et l’Albanie. La France concentre l’essentiel de la participation et des violences. En France, la journée du samedi 17 octobre est née d’appels à manifester lancés sur les réseaux sociaux contre la hausse des prix des carburants. Les Gilets jaunes, les lycéens et les syndicats s’y sont ensuite ralliés. Le ministère de l’Intérieur fait état d’environ 550 000 manifestants, dont 110 000 à Paris. La CGT, elle, en revendique près de 800 000. Les revendications des manifestants varient selon leur appartenance, allant du coût de la vie à la hausse des salaires et des pensions, en passant par la baisse du prix du carburant, la protection des services publics, les conditions dans les lycées, les emplois du temps surchargés et le manque de professeurs. Le ministre de l'Intérieur, Laurent Nuñez, fait état de plus de 2 000 interpellations et de plus de 600 policiers, gendarmes et pompiers blessés, un bilan qu’il juge provisoire. 1500 de commerces ont été touchés, pillés et vandalisés selon le président de la Fédération du commerce et de la distribution. L’hôtel de ville de Limoges a été en grande partie détruit par un incendie et les mairies de Marseille et de Lille ont été envahies et vandalisées. Une grande journée intersyndicale de grève et de manifestation interprofessionnelle est annoncée pour le 5 novembre. En Belgique, le mouvement du 17 octobre s'inscrit dans le cadre de plusieurs semaines de manifestations contre les frais d’inscription à l’université et les coupes budgétaires dans l’éducation. Les syndicats s’opposent également aux mesures envisagées par le gouvernement belge, qui peine à faire adopter son projet de budget. À Bruxelles, le cortège a dégénéré en émeutes peu avant 13 heures : le siège de la fédération bruxelloise du PS a été attaqué. Quelque 150 personnes ont été interpellées, selon Le Soir. En Italie, des milliers de personnes sont descendues dans les rues de Milan, Turin et Bologne et à Rome pour dénoncer les bas salaires et le coût de la vie. Dans le sud du pays, les routiers et les agriculteurs ont également manifesté pour protester contre la hausse du prix du carburant. Selon l’agence de presse Ansa, citant la police, 28 personnes ont été arrêtées dans tout le pays, dont 12 mineurs, et 141 policiers ont été blessés. Au Portugal, les manifestations font suite à une opération policière menée en début de semaine pour évacuer un campement de protestataires contre la crise du logement à Porto. Selon les organisateurs, cette opération aurait fait environ 40 blessés. Les manifestations se sont transformées en une campagne nationale contre les loyers inabordables, les bas salaires et la hausse des prix des produits alimentaires et du carburant. En Albanie, les manifestations se poursuivent pour dénoncer la corruption, le manque d’emplois et le manque de moyens dans le système éducatif. Ces protestations font suite à des mois de manifestations pacifiques durant l'été contre un projet touristique de luxe soutenu par le gendre de Donald Trump, Jared Kushner. Ces mouvements, aussi distincts soient-ils, partagent plusieurs traits communs, dont les difficultés liées à la hausse du coût de la vie. Lycéens et étudiants sont d’ailleurs au cœur des mobilisations en France, en Belgique et en Albanie. De plus, en toile de fond, il y a le choc énergétique qui tire l’inflation vers le haut et qui découle notamment de la guerre que les États-Unis mènent contre l’Iran depuis le 28 février, un conflit sur lequel les pays européens ont très peu de prise. Ces revendications interviennent également dans un contexte fiscal particulièrement fragile, où les marges budgétaires des gouvernements européens pour y répondre sont très limitées. L’article Au-delà de la France, la crise du coût de la vie embrase l’Europe est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: Mali: Military Attacks on Civilians, Insurgent Abuses
items.description: Click to expand Image Screenshot of a video posted online and analyzed by Human Rights Watch showing the destruction of a health center following an apparent Malian military drone strike in Talahandak village in the northern Kidal region, Mali, on July 29, 2026. © Private Malian armed forces and their allies have since July 2026 responded to mounting attacks by Islamist and separatist armed groups with abusive counterinsurgency operations in central and northern Mali.The Malian military, armed groups, and insurgent forces are committing grave laws-of-war violations while international organizations and governments largely stand by.The AU Peace and Security Council should undertake sustained scrutiny of all parties to Mali’s conflict by convening a dedicated session on civilian protection and accountability and pressing them to halt abuses. (Nairobi) – Malian armed forces and their allies have since July 2026 responded to mounting attacks by Islamist and separatist armed groups with abusive counterinsurgency operations in central and northern Mali, Human Rights Watch said today. Mali’s military and the allied Russia-controlled Africa Corps (formally the Wagner Group) have killed and wounded scores of civilians in attacks and in custody in violation of international humanitarian law. Islamist and separatist fighters have also violated the laws-of-war, including torturing and executing captured Malian soldiers. The African Union Peace and Security Council should urgently take action to prevent further atrocities in Mali. “The Malian military, armed groups, and insurgent forces are committing grave laws-of-war violations while international organizations and governments largely stand by,” said Ilaria Allegrozzi, senior Sahel researcher at Human Rights Watch. “The AU Peace and Security Council should undertake sustained scrutiny of all parties to Mali’s conflict by convening a dedicated session on civilian protection and accountability and pressing them to halt abuses.” Between July 30 and September 20, 2026, Human Rights Watch remotely interviewed 30 people, including 16 witnesses to abuses, human rights defenders, community leaders, journalists, and a Malian soldier. Human Rights Watch verified and geolocated two videosposted online showing the aftermath of an apparent drone strike and analyzed 12 photographs of the drone’s debris. Human Rights Watch also reviewed photographs and videos of casualties from other incidents documented. Human Rights Watch sent a letter to Mali’s defense minister on August 5 with findings and questions but received no response. Human Rights Watch documented two apparently indiscriminate Malian military drone attacks: a strike on July 29 in Talahandak village, in the northern Kidal region, that partially destroyed a health facility; and another one on August 19 at a market in Tombonkore village, in the central Bandiagara region, that killed six civilians and injured at least 20 others. Human Rights Watch also documented that on July 12 Malian soldiers shot and killed five girls during a counterinsurgency operation in the central Ségou region, and that on July 27 and 28, allied Dozo militia killed three civilians in the central Mopti region, all with impunity. The Al-Qaeda-linked Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims (Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin, or JNIM) and allied separatist fighters of the Azawad Liberation Front (Front de libération de l’Azawad, or FLA) attacked a military convoy on July 18 in Gao region and then tortured and executed at least 19 Malian troops taken prisoner. These incidents occurred amid renewed fighting in Mali. On April 25, JNIM carried out coordinated attacks across the country alongside FLA fighters seeking to overthrow the military junta led by Gen. Assimi Goïta and backed by the Africa Corps. Malian armed forces and their allies responded with airstrikes that killed civilians and with reprisals against ethnic communities accused of collaborating with the insurgents. “I found myself on the ground, propelled by the blast, stuck between a cart and a tree more than 15 meters from where I had been,” said a 24-year-old man who survived the August 19 attack. “Everyone started running. I tried to get up and saw that my right leg was completely shredded. Blood was dripping from my pants.” Since their coordinated attacks in April, JNIM and the FLA have captured and detained increasing numbers of Malian security personnel. Concerns over their treatment intensified after the two armed groups claimed responsibility for a July 18 attack against a Malian military and Africa Corps convoy in Tabrichat, Gao region, in which at least 19 Malian troops who had surrendered were tortured and executed. Human Rights Watch reviewed videos posted online, also previously analyzed by Amnesty International, showing armed men beating and shooting surrendering soldiers. Human Rights Watch could not determine whether the armed men were JNIM or FLA fighters. However, in one of the videos, credible sources and international media identified one of the men as the son of JNIM’s leader, Iyad Ag Ghali. In at least two videos, as Amnesty International highlighted, a white flag with black writing, characteristic of JNIM, is visible on the front of the attackers’ vehicles. “Once [we made it to] Gao, over 50 military personnel were missing,” a soldier who survived the attack said. “At least 19 were executed – we saw them in the videos. The others? Dead? Captured? We don’t know. We can’t ask questions and we have been prohibited from watching the videos in the camp.” JNIM’s Sharia Committee, in a September 30 response (English, Arabic) to Human Rights Watch, wrote that “although the killing of captives in Tabrichat … did in fact take place, we did not give the order for it, not because it is not permitted in our religion, but because we considered it a matter of interest to leave this alone.” JNIM added that Islam “grants Muslim leaders four choices with respect to captives: release, ransom, enslavement, and execution … even though we did not order our troops to commit that incident and it is not our policy to do such things, what they did does not violate our Sharia such that we see it necessary to hold them accountable or punish them.” In a September 20 response to Human Rights Watch, Mohamed Elmaouloud Ramadane, FLA’s spokesperson, wrote that “[t]he FLA acknowledges that armed clashes took place between its forces and those of the Malian army and its Russian allies of the Africa Corps in Tabrichat on July 18, … However, the FLA categorically rejects any allegation that its forces carried out the execution” of Malian soldiers. He added that “the FLA has carried out and will continue to carry out … internal checks about any … violations of international humanitarian law by some of its members … especially those from Tabrichat.” All parties to Mali’s armed conflict are bound by international humanitarian law, notably Common Article 3, Protocol Additional of 1977 to the 1949 Geneva Conventions relating to the Protection of Victims of Non-International Armed Conflicts (Protocol II), and customary laws-of-war. Deliberate or indiscriminate attacks on civilians or civilian property, including medical facilities, are prohibited. Indiscriminate attacks include those that do not target a specific military objective. Common Article 3 and Protocol II also provide that anyone deprived of their liberty must be treated humanely in all circumstances. In particular, they are protected against murder, torture, and cruel, humiliating, and degrading treatment. Individuals who commit serious violations of the laws-of-war with criminal intent or are responsible as a matter of command responsibility may be prosecuted for war crimes. At its April 28 session on Mali, the AU Peace and Security Council called for protecting civilians and regular briefings and requested increased AU support for Mali’s security sector in compliance with international human rights and humanitarian law. The council should follow through by adopting a communiqué condemning abuses by all parties to the conflict and requesting an urgent report on civilian protection measures and investigations, Human Rights Watch said. “The AU Peace and Security Council should follow up its commitments to protect civilians in Mali with concrete measures and regular public reporting,” Allegrozzi said. “It should press the Malian authorities to conduct independent investigations into abuses by the Malian military and its allies as well as opposition forces, and offer support in such investigations from AU human rights experts.” Abuses by Malian Armed Forces and Allied Militias Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED), a nongovernmental organization that monitors, collects, and analyzes conflict-related data globally, reported that between April and August 2026, Malian forces and the Africa Corps carried out 49 airstrikes, killing 89 civilians, more than double the 22 strikes and 44 civilian deaths reported during the same period in 2025. ACLED data also show that between April and August, the Malian armed forces killed 268 civilians. JNIM forces killed 134 civilians over the same period. Following military coups in 2020 and 2021, Mali’s junta has increasingly used airstrikes in its operations against armed groups. Mali has acquired and used Turkish-made Bayraktar TB2 drones since 2022 and Turkish-made Akinci drones since 2024. Russia has since 2022 also provided drones and fighter jets to Africa Corps personnel in Mali. Human Rights Watch, as well as other human rights groups and several media and investigative organizations, have repeatedly documented unlawfully indiscriminate or disproportionate airstrikes that caused civilian casualties. Apparent Indiscriminate Drone Strikes Tombonkore, Bandiagara Region, August 19 On the morning of August 19, an apparent military drone released munition on civilians gathered at the cattle market in the village of Tombonkore, Kilimpo area, Bandiagara region, killing six men and injuring at least 20 others. The strike also killed several animals and destroyed market stalls and motorbikes. Five witnesses, including three injured in the strike, said that JNIM forces controlled the Tombonkore vicinity, but that no JNIM fighters were at the market or in the village at the time of the strike. They said the drone flew over the village for an extended period before releasing its munition, suggesting that the area was being surveilled. “It [the drone] was gray and slowly flew above us from east to west and back for about 30 minutes before it bombed us,” said a cattle trader, 48, who was at the market. Human Rights Watch could not identify the specific drone or munition used. However, the Malian military and allied Africa Corps are the only known forces in Mali to possess the large drones described by witnesses. A 43-year-old witness said: When the drone dropped the bomb on the market, I was thrown to the ground, blood gushing from my body. I saw my right arm was almost severed, held together only by a tiny piece of flesh. The blood was flowing profusely. A man … dragged me toward a small house nearby. I felt excruciating pain, and lay in a pool of blood. I saw people running, I heard screams. I got up after 40 minutes like that, and … looked for help. A man I didn’t know rescued me, took my turban and tied it around my arm securely to stop the bleeding. The man’s arm was later amputated at the hospital in Sévaré. A 24-year-old man injured in the strike was interviewed hours before doctors amputated his right leg at the Sévaré hospital. He said he saw the drone repeatedly fly over the village, first eastward and later westward at increasingly lower altitude, until it approached the village more directly and dropped its munition. He said: I saw people lying down, screaming and asking for help. It was at least an hour later that the villagers came to rescue us. I was rescued by a [ethnic] Dogon [man] who took me to his home next to the market, where I found my wife and other wounded people.… The motorcycle that my friend and I had come with to the market had caught fire. We had no means of transportation.… My foot was wrapped with a big cloth, and the pain was so severe. I spent the night with this Dogon family.… The next day, my foot looked like an elephant’s leg…. They took me to the hospital, and I am waiting for doctors to amputate my leg. A 29-year-old butcher said he was at the market when the drone dropped its munition: I fell and tried to get up, but I couldn’t. I saw blood running from my clothes, but I didn’t feel any pain. I then crawled to take cover under a cart to avoid a second strike. I looked at my leg; it was red with blood and twisted. From there, I saw several people on the ground, some screaming and others not moving. People were running everywhere. Motorcycles parked near my butcher shop caught fire. I was screaming for help, but people were running around, and no one was listening to me. After an hour and a half like that, calm returned, the market was empty, and villagers came to help the injured. I had lost a lot of blood. Friends and a cousin … tied my leg with a cloth before lifting me. I couldn’t breathe; I felt nauseated. The man said that his cousin took him to the hospital in Bandiagara and then to the Sévaré hospital, where his right leg was treated for a fracture. The 48-year-old man said he helped evacuate the injured by putting them on carts and motorcycles and buried the bodies of those killed. He said five civilian men died on the spot, while a sixth died of his injuries at the Sévaré hospital: Around 3 p.m. we buried the dead at the village cemetery, each in his grave.... There were no JNIM fighters among the dead. The bodies of those killed … had deep wounds in the abdomen and back.… The bodies were almost all at the same place, at the market, a few meters one from the other. Fourteen were seriously injured and were taken to either Bandiagara or Sévaré hospitals. Others, with less serious wounds, were treated in the village – they did not want to go to the hospital because they feared reprisals from the FAMA [Malian armed forces]. Among the injured, I saw one who had almost lost an arm, another had both legs in tatters, and others had open wounds on their abdomen, back, and head. Witnesses shared with Human Rights Watch a video showing the aftermath of the strike. Although Human Rights Watch was not able to independently geolocate it, the footage includes an on-screen narration identifying the location and date of the attack consistent with witness accounts. The video shows the bodies of at least two men and blood on the ground. Human Rights Watch also reviewed 10 photographs from witnesses showing one of the bodies visible in the video, another dead man, dead animals, and other people that witnesses said were injured in the strike. One of the photographs shows a man whose right arm is severely damaged; a forensic expert who reviewed the image said that injuries to the arm were highly consistent with a blast injury. Three other photographs show three injured men, with wounds to their legs and arms, including one who sustained a traumatic amputation. The chief of staff of the Malian armed forces issued a statement on August 20 that on the previous day Malian forces and their partners successfully struck a “terrorist hideout” in the Kilimpo area after long monitoring it. He added that about 20 “terrorists” were “neutralized,” and military equipment destroyed. Human Rights Watch reviewed a list provided by witnesses with the names of the six men, ages 21 to 54, killed in the strike. “They [JNIM fighters] weren’t there that day, and still they are often around the village and also visit it,” said the 24-year-old man. “They preach and, above all, they make a lot of purchases at the market, buying fuel, pasta, spices, cereals, especially on Fridays. They also come during the week to make sure everyone follows the rules.” Talahandak, Kidal Region, July 29 On July 29 at about 4 a.m., an apparent one-way (“kamikaze”) attack drone hit and partially destroyed a health center in Talahandak, a village in a JNIM and FLA-controlled area near the Algerian border. Two men, including a 45-year-old health worker who witnessed the explosion, said that no JNIM or FLA fighters were in or around the health facility at the time of the strike and that the health center did not store anything other than medicines and medical equipment. The health worker said: At the health center, we took care of men, women, children, and elderly people suffering from, among other things, malaria. Under no circumstances was this facility used by armed groups.… Only civilians received care here. Today, the center is destroyed.… Women and children, already deprived of basic health services, are going to suffer from this situation, not the armed groups. There were never any munitions or armed vehicles on site, even in the days before the attack. The fighters never came here. No terrorist or armed man was ever treated here; we don’t even have the medical means to treat war injuries. The witnesses said they recovered the drone’s debris. They provided 12 photographs they said were taken at the site after the strike. The photographs analyzed by Human Rights Watch show components and remnants consistent with a Shahed-type delta wing drone, including control surfaces, brackets, bolt patterns, and internal construction. In a July 24 report, Bellingcat and Jeune Afrique geolocated footage showing Shahed-136 type one-way attack drones in operation in Mali. They verified two strikes, including one in Talahandak on July 17 that destroyed a truck carrying cooking oil and killed one civilian. A 35-year-old resident of Talahandak said: The health center was hit. The pharmacy and the room where the patients used to get treated were destroyed, as well as the patients’ beds, the lab equipment, and the pharmaceutical products. It’s completely in ruins and can’t be used for anything anymore. I can’t accurately describe the drone because it was dark. But I heard it and saw the strike, the explosion, the flames, and the fire coming from the health center. The drone sounded like a motorcycle, came at full speed, and crashed straight into its target. The next day, we went to see the ruins of the health center. We saw the drone’s engine as well as its propeller, which were not too damaged. Human Rights Watch also verified and geolocated two videos posted to X on July 29 showing the interior and exterior of the Talahandak health center. The footage shows extensive damage to several rooms identified as the men’s and women’s treatment rooms, the laboratory, the pharmacy, and a consultation and ultrasound room. Damaged medical equipment and supplies are visible throughout the facility. The room marked as the men’s treatment room appears to be the most damaged, with a large hole in its exterior wall where a window had been. Debris is scattered through the room, and numerous fragmentation impacts are visible on the walls, along with signs of fire damage, and a charred stretcher. The videos also show structural damage to at least two of the building’s facades and its roof. Human Rights Watch also analyzed satellite imagery from August 6 that showed severe damage to the roof’s northwestern corner. Under international humanitarian law, all medical facilities are protected from attack, including facilities that treat members of belligerent armed forces or armed groups. This protection ceases only when medical facilities are used to commit hostile acts outside their humanitarian function, and then only after a warning that goes unheeded. Abuses During Counterinsurgency Operations Djenné, Mopti Region, July 27 and 28 On July 27 around noon, a militia member from a group of dozens of Dozo militiamen wearing traditional clothing and armed with Kalashnikov-style assault rifles shot and killed a 50-year-old ethnic Fulani man near the main mosque in Djenné. Minutes later, the militiamen fatally shot another Fulani man, 43, at the same location. A 45-year-old resident said: During the attack, I was with my friend [the 43-year-old man]. We were together when we heard a gunshot. I immediately told him, ‘Let’s take cover, it’s right next to us.’ He hesitated while I ran without waiting. The Dozo then shot him. In fact, the very first gunshot we heard was aimed at another friend of mine [the 50-year-old man]. The Dozo killed him, and we saw him collapse. When I turned my head, I saw a large group of Dozo, armed with Kalashnikovs, heading toward us. I personally know them because we all live in Djenné. To save myself, I had to run and leave my friend behind. That’s when they shot him. Another witness provided a similar description of the incident. On July 28, four Dozo militiamen, believed to be members of the same group who entered Djenné the previous day, forced their way into a house in Sankore neighborhood. They dragged out a 42-year-old Fulani man, tied his hands behind his back, blindfolded him, and drove away with him. His relatives found his body the next day, about two kilometers away, with three gunshot wounds to the head and chest. Human Rights Watch spoke to two witnesses to the abduction, including the victim’s 32-year-old wife. She said that on the day the Dozo shot and killed the two men near the mosque, fear spread throughout Djenné’s Fulani community, prompting many to flee. She said she urged her husband to flee, but he refused, saying that he had spoken with the military based in town to report the incident and seek protection. The wife said: The next day, on July 28, around 10 a.m., four Dozo armed with Kalashnikovs, dressed in their traditional outfits and horned hats, surrounded our house.... Two of them broke inside the house and forcibly took him [the husband] out. They grabbed his turban to blindfold him, tied his hands behind his back, put him on a motorcycle, and drove off with him. That’s the last time I saw him alive. The other witness, a 39-year-old man, was among the people who found the victim’s body, “under a tree [with] a bullet wound in the head and two in his chest.” Residents said that there were no JNIM fighters in Djenné on the days of the killings and the abduction. They said the victims were targeted because they were Fulani. Islamist armed groups, including JNIM, have long recruited from Fulani communities in the area. Malian authorities and allied ethnic militias have repeatedly equated Fulani civilians with Islamist fighters to justify killings and other serious abuses. Niono, Ségou Region, July 12 On July 12 at about 3 p.m., Malian soldiers shot and killed five girls, ages 10 to 13, who were harvesting rice in a field about three kilometers from Niono town. The soldiers took the victims’ bodies to the morgue at Niono hospital and later apologized to their families, acknowledging that they had made a mistake. They said that earlier that day, around midday, they had come under attack approximately nine kilometers away. When they later saw heads emerging from the rice fields, they mistakenly believed they were the attackers and opened fire. The father of three of the victims, a 46-year-old Fulani man, said: When I arrived, the hospital was cordoned off by soldiers. I went inside and a nurse told me, ‘The soldiers brought the children’s bodies here.’ … The nurse confirmed the children had been shot by the army […] and then he led me to the morgue. That’s where I found my three children lying, their bodies riddled with bullets. Devastated, I asked the nurse, “What happened to them? They were just kids going to work in the fields, they weren’t fighting in any war! Why are they coming back like this?” “An army captain came all the way to our home in person to apologize to us,” said the father of the two other victims, a 59-year-old ethnic Dogon man. “He told us that they were completely sorry and that their intention was never to kill children.” The other father said he received a similar explanation from the soldiers. It is evident that the soldiers did not do everything feasible to verify that the targets of the attack were combatants, resulting in the killing of civilians in violation of the laws-of-war. As of mid-September, the government had not, to Human Rights Watch’s knowledge, opened an investigation into this incident, nor had the families been offered any reparations. Abuses by JNIM and FLA Armed Groups Tabrichat, Gao Region, July 18 On July 18, JNIM and FLA fighters attacked a Malian military and Africa Corps convoy traveling from Anefis to the city of Gao near Tabrichat village in the Gao region. Both armed groups claimed responsibility for the attack, with JNIM noting “heavy casualties and significant material damage to the enemy,” and the FLA stating there were “heavy losses on the enemy side, several dead left on the battlefield, dozens of injured as well as prisoners.” International media and human rights organizations reported that the armed groups captured dozens of Malian soldiers, tortured several, and then executed many. Radio France Internationale reported that JNIM and FLA fighters “summarily executed Malian soldiers who had surrendered.” Amnesty International documented the beating and abuse of the captured soldiers by alleged JNIM and FLA fighters and the execution of at least 19. Human Rights Watch spoke to a Malian soldier who was in the convoy and with two victims’ relatives and reviewed videos posted on social media previously analyzed by Amnesty International. The videos show surrendering soldiers with their hands in the air or clasped behind their heads walking in the desert surrounded by armed men and their vehicles. Armed men can be seen beating and shooting at the captured soldiers. On July 23, the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights condemned the torture and killing of surrendered soldiers in Tabrichat and called for accountability. The Malian soldier said the convoy left Anefis at about 10 p.m. on July 17, bound for Gao. Africa Corps fighters, he said, led the convoy, followed by soldiers from the Aguelhokcamp. Soldiers from the Anefis base were at the rear. He said that right from the convoy’s departure, he was worried by “the huge lack of coordination between the Africa Corps, the Anefis units, and the few units that came from Aguelhok.” The soldier said: Breakdowns and flat tires were too frequent, while FLA and JNIM fighters were following us since we left the camp. We were intercepting their communications. They clearly intended to attack the convoy before the morning. The terrorists had surveillance drones and launched rockets at the convoy…. Near Tabrichat, everyone understood that the convoy would be attacked and that when the attack happened, nobody would be able to counter it because we were slowed down by the breakdowns and flat tires and lacked any real coordination. We didn’t know who was where, who was doing what, who was on defense, and who was dealing with the broken-down and stuck vehicles. He said that JNIM and FLA fighters attacked the convoy at about 7 a.m. in Tabrichat, in a sandy area where vehicles could easily get stuck. The insurgents began surrounding the convoy and split it into two groups. He said Africa Corps fighters in front did not turn back to help, escaping instead. Malian soldiers at the middle and rear of the convoy were overwhelmed despite returning fire. “Some managed to escape, others were captured and executed,” he said. “The number of soldiers we counted as missing after the ambush is over 50. Among these 50 soldiers, 19 were executed.” A 32-year-old woman said she learned that her husband, an army sergeant who had been deployed to Anefis since 2023, was killed in the ambush by watching videos that circulated online soon after the attack. She said: I began struggling to breathe. I immediately left the hairdresser—who had shown me the images—to go to the military camp [in Gao].… I asked a soldier if he knew about the ambush and he replied: ‘Yes, but the situation is under control.’ … I told him I identified my husband in the videos … but he told me not to pay attention to fake videos produced by the JNIM and FLA’s propaganda [outlets], which are ‘aimed at discouraging and demoralizing the military.’ He told me to go back home and wait for an official military communication. The woman said the following day she spoke to her husband’s brother who told her he had also gone to see the military in Gao but had received the same answers. They then decided to seek more information from an FLA commander. She said: We wrote him the following message: ‘Was our military relative among the soldiers who were attacked in Tabrichat? Can you verify if he’s still alive?’ The rebel commander immediately responded that the FLA did not execute any soldiers but only took them prisoner and brought them to a safe place [but] a military drone bombed the place and all prisoners died. He added that if our relative was among those taken prisoner, we should not assume that he would come back home.… It was at this moment that I began mourning. In response to Human Rights Watch’s query, the FLA’s spokesperson, Mohamed Elmaouloud Ramadane, also suggested that drone strikes had killed the soldiers in the custody of the rebel groups: “[S]everal military personnel under the control of or near FLA forces were killed following drone strikes carried out by the Malian armed forces and their Russian Africa Corps allies after the clashes.” In a July 18 statement, the chief of staff of the Malian armed forces said that “alongside the air and ground response launched to support the convoy attacked in Tabrichat by the JNIM/FLA terrorist coalition, the Malian armed forces are continuing their operations ... across the country.” The media reported that the public prosecutor at the judicial unit specializing in terrorism cases and organized transnational crime announced on August 1 the opening of an investigation into the summary executions at Tabrichat. As of mid-September, the Malian army had not contacted the families of the soldiers killed or missing to provide information or support. A carpenter whose brother, a 37-year-old soldier, has been missing since the Tabrichat attack, said that he had identified him in one of the videos that circulated online: The day after the ambush, we watched the videos and we identified him. He and his comrades can be seen with their hands up, one after the other, surrounded by the armed groups.… Any attempt to get more information from the army was in vain. His surviving comrades refused to tell us more about what happened that day. So, we have to mourn and leave it in God’s hands. He added that no authorities contacted him or his family to provide information about Tabrichat: I learned that the government has opened an investigation, but ... no government official has come to ask us anything.... The government has never reached out to us. Neither to offer condolences nor to talk to us about the investigation.… Authorities have shut themselves off in silence about this incident, and in this specific situation where soldiers are captured, executed, and filmed, relatives deserve answers. Human Rights Watch reviewed a list, shared by the soldier and victims’ relatives, with the names of five soldiers believed killed in the attack, ages 37 to 52.

items.title: Commerce maritime mondial : qui contrôle les ports, les navires et les grandes routes ?
items.description: Shanghai, Singapour, Ningbo-Zhoushan… Les principaux ports à conteneurs se concentrent en Asie, tandis que les grandes compagnies maritimes sont dominées par des groupes européens. La propriété des flottes marchandes dessine, elle, une autre géographie du pouvoir économique mondial. Lorsqu’un grand port cesse de fonctionner ou qu’une route maritime est perturbée, les conséquences dépassent largement les quais et les terminaux concernés. Les retards d’acheminement peuvent désorganiser des chaînes de production, priver des commerces de marchandises et contraindre les entreprises à engager des dépenses supplémentaires pour sécuriser leurs approvisionnements. À l’autre bout de la chaîne, les consommateurs peuvent subir une hausse des prix sans toujours mesurer le rôle du transport maritime dans le coût des produits qu’ils achètent. Les crises qui ont affecté le commerce maritime ces dernières années ont mis en lumière la vulnérabilité d’un système fondé sur l’interconnexion des ports, des armateurs et des grandes routes commerciales. Une perturbation dans un passage stratégique ou une plateforme majeure peut se répercuter sur les échanges entre les continents, renchérir les coûts de production et alimenter les tensions sur les prix. L’enjeu est considérable. Selon les estimations de la Conférence des Nations unies sur le commerce et le développement (CNUCED), environ 80 % du commerce mondial de marchandises, en volume, est acheminé par voie maritime. Les ports, les navires et les infrastructures qui les relient constituent ainsi des éléments essentiels du fonctionnement de l’économie mondiale. Mais le contrôle de ces flux ne se concentre pas entre les mains des mêmes acteurs. Les pays qui accueillent les plus grands ports ne sont pas nécessairement ceux dont les entreprises exploitent les principales flottes de porte-conteneurs. De même, les États qui possèdent les plus importantes flottes marchandes ne se confondent pas avec les centres majeurs de manutention des marchandises. Trois cartes permettent de comprendre cette répartition du pouvoir maritime. 1. Les ports asiatiques au cœur des échanges mondiaux La domination asiatique est particulièrement nette dans le secteur des conteneurs. L’essor industriel et exportateur de la Chine, conjugué au rôle des plateformes de transbordement, a consolidé la position de plusieurs ports de la région. Singapour et Busan, en Corée du Sud, jouent notamment un rôle important dans la connexion des lignes maritimes internationales. Les données de 2025 confirment cette concentration : la Chine occupe six des dix premières places mondiales en matière de trafic de conteneurs. Shanghai conserve la première position, devant Singapour, qui demeure l’un des principaux centres de transbordement maritime de la planète. Selon le volume annuel de manutention, le port de Shanghai arrive en tête avec 55,06 millions d’EVP, devant Singapour, qui en totalise 44,66 millions, et Ningbo-Zhoushan, en Chine, avec 43,87 millions. Shenzhen occupe la quatrième place avec 35,41 millions d’EVP, suivi de Qingdao, avec 34,20 millions, et de Guangzhou, avec 28,05 millions. Le port sud-coréen de Busan se classe septième avec 24,88 millions d’EVP, devant Tianjin, en Chine, qui en enregistre 24,03 millions. Jebel Ali, aux Émirats arabes unis, occupe la neuvième place avec environ 15,6 millions d’EVP, tandis que Port Klang, en Malaisie, ferme le classement avec près de 15,1 millions d’EVP. L’EVP, ou équivalent vingt pieds, est l’unité de référence utilisée pour mesurer le trafic et la capacité des conteneurs maritimes. Cette prépondérance chinoise ne reflète pas uniquement le poids de son économie. Elle traduit également l’importance des infrastructures portuaires dans la compétitivité des exportations. Grâce à son vaste réseau de ports et à la diversité des lignes maritimes qui les desservent, la Chine dispose de plusieurs voies d’acheminement pour ses produits industriels et ses matières premières. Cette multiplicité des connexions contribue à limiter la dépendance à un itinéraire unique. La concentration du trafic dans les ports asiatiques ne signifie toutefois pas que l’ensemble de la chaîne maritime soit contrôlé par les économies de la région. L’exploitation des navires et l’organisation des lignes régulières obéissent à une autre logique, dominée par un nombre restreint de grandes compagnies internationales. Trois compagnies européennes concentrent près de la moitié des capacités mondiales Les ports assurent le passage des marchandises, mais les armateurs organisent leur circulation entre les marchés. À travers leurs flottes, leurs lignes régulières et leurs réseaux logistiques, les compagnies maritimes déterminent une part importante des capacités disponibles et des itinéraires empruntés par les cargaisons. Les données d’ Alphaliner , organisme spécialisé dans le suivi des flottes de porte-conteneurs, mettent en évidence la concentration du secteur. Le groupe suisse Mediterranean Shipping Company (MSC) occupe la première place mondiale, avec une capacité supérieure à un cinquième de celle des flottes de porte-conteneurs exploitées dans le monde. Il devance le danois Maersk et le français CMA CGM. MSC arrive en tête avec une capacité de 7,45 millions d’EVP, devant Maersk, qui dispose de 4,73 millions d’EVP, et CMA CGM, avec 4,47 millions. Le chinois COSCO occupe la quatrième place avec 3,68 millions d’EVP, suivi de l’allemand Hapag-Lloyd, avec 2,41 millions, et de la compagnie Ocean Network Express (ONE), basée à Singapour, avec 2,19 millions. Le groupe taïwanais Evergreen se classe septième avec 2,04 millions d’EVP, devant le sud-coréen HMM, qui totalise 1,03 million. Yang Ming, également taïwanais, dispose d’une capacité de 771 000 EVP, tandis que l’israélien ZIM ferme le classement avec 691 000 EVP. Cette hiérarchie contraste avec celle des infrastructures portuaires. Alors que la Chine occupe six des dix premières places mondiales pour la manutention des conteneurs, les trois principaux exploitants de porte-conteneurs ont leur siège en Europe. La répartition des rôles distingue ainsi les économies qui concentrent une part importante de la production et des exportations des groupes qui organisent l’acheminement des marchandises à l’échelle internationale. MSC, Maersk et CMA CGM représentent ensemble environ 48 % de la capacité mondiale des flottes de porte-conteneurs en exploitation. Une telle concentration confère à leurs décisions relatives à l’affectation des navires et à l’organisation des lignes une importance qui dépasse leurs seules activités commerciales, particulièrement lorsque des routes maritimes stratégiques sont perturbées. Cette position ne leur permet pas pour autant de fixer unilatéralement les tarifs du fret. Les prix dépendent de plusieurs variables : la demande de transport, les capacités disponibles, les cours du carburant, la congestion des ports, les coûts d’exploitation et la concurrence entre les compagnies, notamment au sein des alliances maritimes. La puissance des armateurs constitue donc un élément central de la chaîne logistique mondiale, sans être le seul facteur déterminant des conditions d’acheminement des marchandises. La Grèce, première puissance mondiale en matière de propriété de navires marchands La hiérarchie change encore lorsque l’on ne s’intéresse plus aux seuls porte-conteneurs, mais à l’ensemble de la flotte marchande. Celle-ci comprend des navires transportant du pétrole, du gaz, des céréales, du charbon et des minerais, mais aussi des bâtiments spécialisés dans le transport de véhicules et de marchandises diverses. Dans ce domaine, la Grèce occupe la première place mondiale en matière de port en lourd de la flotte marchande détenue par ses entreprises et ses investisseurs. Elle devance la Chine et le Japon, alors même que les ports grecs ne figurent pas parmi les principaux centres mondiaux de manutention des conteneurs. Le port en lourd correspond au poids total qu’un navire peut transporter, notamment les marchandises, le carburant et les approvisionnements. Cet indicateur permet de comparer la capacité des flottes marchandes en tenant compte de la taille des navires, contrairement au simple décompte des bâtiments. La Grèce arrive en tête avec 397,65 millions de tonnes de port en lourd, devant la Chine, avec 347,22 millions de tonnes, et le Japon, avec 240,68 millions. Singapour occupe la quatrième place avec 153,43 millions de tonnes, suivi de Hong Kong, rattaché à la Chine, avec 139,50 millions. La Corée du Sud se classe sixième avec 98,53 millions de tonnes, devant l’Allemagne, avec 71,53 millions, et Taïwan, avec 63,88 millions. Les Émirats arabes unis arrivent en neuvième position avec 57,43 millions de tonnes, tandis que le Royaume-Uni et l’île de Man ferment le classement avec 56,99 millions de tonnes. Selon la CNUCED, les dix premiers pays propriétaires représentent ensemble environ 67,3 % du port en lourd de la flotte marchande mondiale. La Grèce, la Chine et le Japon en concentrent à eux seuls plus de 40 %. Cette répartition appelle toutefois une distinction entre la propriété des navires et leur pavillon d’immatriculation. Un navire enregistré dans un pays n’appartient pas nécessairement à une entreprise de cet État. Les compagnies maritimes peuvent choisir d’immatriculer leurs bâtiments dans d’autres juridictions, notamment au Liberia, au Panama ou aux îles Marshall, en fonction des réglementations, de la fiscalité et des conditions d’exploitation. Le pavillon ne suffit donc pas, à lui seul, à déterminer la nationalité économique du propriétaire d’un navire. Cette distinction est essentielle pour comprendre la véritable géographie du secteur maritime. Une puissance maritime répartie entre plusieurs centres de décision La cartographie du commerce maritime mondial fait apparaître une répartition des rôles entre plusieurs ensembles géographiques. L’Asie concentre la majorité des grands ports à conteneurs, tandis que les principales capacités d’exploitation de ces navires sont dominées par trois groupes européens. Dans le domaine plus large de la flotte marchande, la Grèce, la Chine et le Japon occupent les premières positions. Ces différents classements révèlent que la puissance maritime ne se mesure pas à un seul indicateur. Le trafic manutentionné dans les ports, la capacité des flottes de porte-conteneurs et le port en lourd des navires marchands correspondent à des réalités distinctes. Ils éclairent chacun une dimension du contrôle des échanges internationaux. Cette organisation repose sur une interdépendance croissante entre les infrastructures, les compagnies et les routes commerciales. Les ports ont besoin des navires pour écouler les marchandises, tandis que les armateurs dépendent des infrastructures portuaires pour assurer leurs rotations et maintenir leurs réseaux logistiques. Cette interconnexion rend le commerce mondial plus efficace, mais elle accroît aussi sa sensibilité aux perturbations. Lorsqu’un passage stratégique ou un grand centre maritime est affecté, les répercussions peuvent se propager à l’ensemble de la chaîne d’approvisionnement, des sites de production jusqu’aux marchés de consommation. La capacité à maintenir la continuité des échanges dépend ainsi moins de la domination d’un acteur unique que du fonctionnement coordonné de plusieurs centres de décision. C’est dans cette interdépendance que réside à la fois la force du transport maritime mondial et l’une de ses principales vulnérabilités. The post Commerce maritime mondial : qui contrôle les ports, les navires et les grandes routes ? appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Despite inflation trend down, stocks sustain losses amid selling pressure
items.description: The Nigerian Exchange Limited, NGX dropped further Week-on-Week, WoW, amid selling pressure across sectors despite the fourth consecutive month of decline in headline inflation rate for the month of September 2026. Specifically, the NGX market capitalisation, which represents the total value of equities listed on the Exchange, dropped to N260.725 trillion last Friday from N161.260 trillion the previous week, as investors lost over N535 billion. Similarly, another market gauge, NGX All Share Index, ASI nosedived by 0.3% to close last Friday at 247539.73 points from 248,363.55 points the previous week. Analysis of trading showed that the market closed lower for the third consecutive week, as losses in Zenith Bank by -6 .5%, MTN Nigeria -1.8%, First HoldCo -3.9% and GTCO -4.4% contributed significantly to drag the ASI down WoW, bringing the Month-to-Date, MtD and Year-to-Date, YtD returns to -1.5% and +59.1%, respectively. On market activity, trading volume and value declined by 39.0% WoW and 38.0% WoW, respectively. On sector performance, the Banking declined by -3.1% and Insurance Index -0.1% , while the Oil & Gas Index rose by 3.1% and Consumer Goods 0.1% respectively. The Industrial Goods index closed flat. Commenting on the market outlook, analysts at Cordros Capital Limited, stated: “Looking ahead, we expect market sentiment to improve, supported by bargain hunting following recent price declines. Secondly, anticipation of third quarter, Q3 earnings releases and positioning ahead of upcoming dividend qualification dates, which could drive selective buying interest.” On their part, analysts at InvestData Consulting Limited, said: “The oil market’s movements may also influence expectations regarding inflation, energy costs and broader economic activity. Changes in crude prices can affect transportation, production and distribution costs, with potential implications for businesses across several sectors. However, the implications for individual companies will vary according to their exposure to energy prices, operating structures and ability to pass higher costs on to customers. Investors should therefore assess the potential impact of oil-price movements within the context of individual company fundamentals and the wider economic environment.” The post Despite inflation trend down, stocks sustain losses amid selling pressure appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Eating grass for AI
items.description: “WE will eat grass or leaves, even go hungry, but we will get one of our own … We have no other choice!” Zulfikar Ali Bhutto had famously remarked as he voiced this nation’s determination to build an indigenous nuclear deterrent programme that had, by the mid-1960s, become an existential necessity. Some seven years later, Pakistan made it a policy imperative. That one call guaranteed the future security of the republic. Decades later, working through sheer grit and determination, Pakistan showed the world that it was more than capable of looking after itself. We stand at a very similar juncture today. The ongoing arms race in AI threatens to upend the global economic and security order, and the turning point is likely to arrive well before we will be prepared to confront it. That is, unless we once again take control of our destiny and start shaping it with our own hands today. A large part of our annual $4.6bn in IT exports is freelancing work, call centres, and entry-level coding, which modern AI directly imperils. At the rate at which the technology is progressing, it will rapidly render many of those services and products either low-value or useless. There is also the question of what we, as an economy, must pay in terms of compute bills if our companies continue to license AI usage from foreign corporations. As dependence on AI grows, the bill could reach hundreds of millions of dollars by the end of the decade. At most critical risk is our defence infrastructure, where drones, electronic warfare, and high-end sensors already run on AI technology, and are only going to grow more dependent on it to maintain their efficacy. The national leadership must, therefore, make haste. In the 1970s, Pakistan was able to offer expat talent a compelling reason to return. Similar arrangements need to be made once again. Talented computer scientists and experts from around the world must be called home, given a deadline, generous budgets, and autonomy. The systems and data centres can be placed close to where power is cheap and stable, while the research can take place where our universities are. A realistic target would be to host open-weight models at home, have researchers and technologists fine-tune them on Pakistani data and languages, run all government and defence needs within the country, and own the data pipelines as well. This would make Pakistan sovereign enough in AI without requiring a frontier-level lab or the 100-billion-dollar budgets that they need. We can build on our ambitions once the basics are in place. The Chagai test took more than two decades; the clock on AI runs much faster than that. Pakistan cannot afford to delay this project. The downside risks are too great. Published in Dawn, October 19th, 2026

items.title: IMF team expected in Ghana this week; 2027 Budget, energy debts in focus
items.description: An International Monetary Fund (IMF) mission is expected in Accra this week for Ghana’s first review under the Policy Coordination Instrument (PCI), with preparations for the 2027 Budget expected to feature prominently in discussions. JoyBusiness understands from sources close to the IMF, contacted on the sidelines of the Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, that the mission will be led by Dr Ruben Atoyan and is expected to last two weeks. The engagement is expected to assess Ghana’s economic performance and progress on reforms aimed at sustaining macroeconomic stability. Areas of focus for the visiting IMF team Discussions are likely to centre on the proposed 2027 Budget and its alignment with commitments under the PCI. The team is also expected to examine fiscal performance up to September 2026, including revenue mobilisation and measures to improve government receipts. Other anticipated areas of discussion include the Bank of Ghana’s recapitalisation, banking-sector supervision and the regulation of the wider financial sector. Energy-sector challenges, particularly legacy debts and their implications for public finances, are also expected to feature prominently. The mission is expected to engage government officials, the central bank and other stakeholders before issuing a statement on its findings. Why this mission visit? The visit forms part of Ghana’s engagement with the IMF under the PCI, a non-financing framework intended to help consolidate economic gains and sustain policy reforms. The IMF Executive Board completed the sixth and final review of Ghana’s Extended Credit Facility arrangement on July 27, 2026, and considered the country’s request for a 36-month PCI. IMF statement Although the PCI does not provide direct IMF funding, the review process gives the authorities an opportunity to demonstrate progress on their economic commitments and reinforce confidence among investors and development partners. Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson has previously explained that the framework is intended to anchor Ghana’s next phase of reforms, strengthen economic resilience and support broad-based growth. He said the programme would help preserve gains made under IMF-supported reforms while reinforcing policy credibility and investor confidence. Understanding the Policy Coordination Instrument The PCI allows countries to maintain close policy engagement with the IMF without receiving financing under the instrument. It supports the design and implementation of economic reforms and can help countries signal policy credibility to development partners and private investors. Its objectives include strengthening macroeconomic stability, addressing underlying economic imbalances and building resilience against shocks. Although it provides no direct funding, policies under the PCI must meet standards comparable to those under IMF lending arrangements. Performance is assessed through reviews on a fixed schedule, normally every six months. The instrument requires IMF Executive Board approval, unlike a Staff-Monitored Programme, which is an informal arrangement between IMF staff and a member country. IMF PCI factsheet

items.title: Mangrove loss raises flood, erosion risks along Karachi coast
items.description: Satellite images from 2000 and 2025 show mangroves near Mai Kolachi replaced by reclaimed land.—Courtesy Suparco ISLAMABAD: New satellite images from 2000 and 2025 released by the country’s space agency show a fundamental shift in land cover along Karachi’s coastal zone near the Mai Kolachi Bypass, where mangrove stands and natural tidal creeks have increasingly given way to reclaimed land and urban development. In a note on the development, the Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Comm­ission (Suparco) said areas once characterised by continuous mangrove cover and natural tidal creeks had progressively been converted into reclaimed land and urban plots. “This transformation refle­cts a transition from ecosystem-based coastal protection to hard, land-intensive development. Mangrove removal directly weakens the coastal system’s ability to respond to climate stress,” the agency said. Suparco observed that mangroves played a key role in regulating coastal temperatures, trapping sediments and absorbing atmospheric carbon. Their clearance not only eliminated an important blue-carbon reservoir but also disrupted hydrological connectivity, increasing surface runoff and altering tidal flows, it said. “Over time, this raises the likelihood of localised flooding, shoreline instability and long-term land subsidence. From a climate perspective, the conversion of mangrove wetlands into built-up land represents a loss of natural resilience at a time when sea-level rise and extreme weather events are accelerating,” it said. Unlike engineered structures, mangroves adapt and regenerate, offering protection that strengthens over time. Their replacement with static infrastructure transfers climate risk directly to urban assets and populations, the agency observed. Satellite images from 2000 and 2025 show mangroves near Mai Kolachi replaced by reclaimed land.—Courtesy Suparco When contacted, Senator Sherry Rehman, chairperson of the Senate Standing Committee on Climate Change, declined to comment. Karachi Mayor Murtaza Wahab did not respond to messages. Climate policy specialist Mohammad Saleem Shaikh warned that Pakistan must protect its mangrove forests and natural tidal creeks, stressing that their destruction threatened coastal communities, livelihoods and economic stability. Referring to Suparco’s satellite evidence showing changes along Karachi’s coast near Mai Kolachi Bypass between 2000 and 2025, Mr Shaikh called for urgent measures to prevent further environmental degradation. He said mangroves stored carbon, reduced coastal erosion, weakened storm surges and sustained fisheries and biodiversity. Their loss could increase Pakistan’s vulnerability to rising sea levels, cyclones and other climate-related threats, particularly along Karachi’s coastline and the Indus Delta, he warned. Mr Shaikh urged the federal and Sindh governments to strengthen environmental enforcement, prevent encroachment and ensure that coastal development projects underwent comprehensive environmental assessments. He also called for transparent satellite monitoring, community participation and scientifically planned restoration using native species. He said mangroves should be treated as natural climate infrastructure essential for disaster resilience and future generations. Meanwhile, satellite imagery acquired between 2019 and 2026 and posted on Suparco’s Spa­ce4Cli­mate webpage showed a substantial mangrove afforestation event in the Shah Bandar region of Sujawal. Comparative analysis of 19 Areas of Interest showed a 115pc increase in mangrove forest cover relative to 2019 baseline area of 116.46 hectares. Newly established mangrove vegetation of 151.24 hectares accounted for around 6.5pc of the total 2,321.8-hectare study area. Published in Dawn, October 19th, 2026

items.title: LPG stakeholders seek daily pricing amid soaring rates
items.description: ISLAMABAD: As liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) prices surge following the closure of the Rahimdad-250 border post, market stakeholders on Sunday urged the government to shift from monthly to weekly or daily pricing, in line with petroleum products, and delink rates from Saudi Aramco’s Contract Price (CP). The demand comes ahead of winter, when LPG consumption traditionally rises, increasing the risk of hoarding, blackmarketing and artificial price hikes, particularly in remote and hilly areas. Stakeholders say the LPG policy, unchanged for over a decade, no longer reflects market realities. Although prices are benchmarked to Saudi CP, supplies largely come from Iran, Oman, the UAE and Iraq, including Iranian LPG allegedly routed through alternative sea channels. They argue that advance monthly prices notified by the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) discourage major state-owned enterprises (SOEs) from importing LPG, leaving the market vulnerable to private importers and land-route suppliers amid weak enforcement. Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik and ministry spokesman Zafar Abbas did not respond to written queries. Border closures, outdated pricing and weak oversight fuel LPG market crisis The Ministry of Commerce’s October 16 memorandums withdrawing electronic import form (EIF) exemptions for Iranian imports and shipments to Central Asian Republics (CARs) and Azerbaijan via Iran have further disrupted supplies. More than 4,500 tonnes of LPG are reportedly stranded on the Iranian side. Pakistan consumes nearly two million tonnes of LPG annually, of which 30 per cent is produced domestically and 70pc imported. Of the 1.2 million tonnes imported, around 250,000 tonnes arrive through Port Qasim and nearly one million tonnes through Iranian routes, including Taftan, Mand and Rahimdad-250. Taftan has remained closed for nearly six months over security concerns, while Mand faces intermittent disruptions, increasing reliance on Rahimdad-250. Mohammad Ali Haider, vice chairman of the LPG Marketing Association, representing over 200 companies, said prices rose by Rs100 per kilogram over the weekend following withdrawal of the trade exemption and could climb further without immediate intervention. He said no imports were currently arriving at Saudi CP-based prices. Before the war, Iranian auctioned LPG reached the border at $100-150 per tonne below Saudi CP. War-related insurance and freight premiums have since pushed costs to around $300 per tonne above CP, making Ogra’s benchmark increasingly unrealistic. Mr Haider said oil prices had shifted to daily adjustments after the war began, while LPG remained tied to advance monthly notifications disconnected from actual costs. Consequently, major players, including SSGC, SNGPL and Pak-Arab Refinery, avoid imports at notified rates, fearing accountability investigations. Border disruptions have also shifted pressure to Gwadar, pushing freight costs from $60-80 to as high as $380 per tonne. Mr Haider alleged that manipulated freight arrangements, questionable import declarations and the absence of digital tracking of tankers, transporters and distributors facilitated profiteering and tax evasion. He also criticised a petroleum division directive requiring SOEs to auction LPG against signature bonuses, arguing that the mechanism favoured cash-rich companies. Pakistan Petroleum Limited had previously allocated production through transparent bidding, offering 25 tonnes monthly to each successful bidder. A relatively obscure company reportedly offered a Rs220 million signature bonus for a five-tonne quota, prompting allegations of money laundering and consumer exploitation. Litigation has stalled the process. Mr Haider urged the government to review the LPG policy with stakeholders, revise the Rs35,000-per-tonne marketing margin fixed in 2016, digitally track imports and distribution, and publish daily prices on Ogra’s website. He also questioned the use of a Rs4,690-per-tonne petroleum levy introduced in 2016 to cushion consumers against price shocks, saying it was not serving its intended purpose. Published in Dawn, October 19th, 2026

Oil tumbles as Trump’s Russia sanctions waiver may lead to more fuel supplies
items.description: Oil prices slipped on Monday after US President Donald Trump waived sanctions and tariffs on Russia, which may lead to more Russian fuel exports. Brent crude futures fell $1.94, or 1.77%, to $107.92 a barrel by 0227 GMT after settling at its highest since May 19 on Friday. US West Texas Intermediate crude was at $100.58 a ​barrel, down 83 cents, or 0.82%, after closing at its highest since September 17 on Friday. Trump ​signed an executive order on Friday waiving key sanctions and tariffs under the law ⁠known as the Graham Act, which he signed last month at the urging of lawmakers who wanted to pressure ​Moscow over its war in Ukraine. However, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the president will use up to ​60 days to assess the economic impact of the sanctions and tariffs on the global economy. The move comes after Trump struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to export diesel to the United States and other countries — starting at about 2.3 million barrels this month and rising to about 7.6 million barrels per month, according to Trump’s announcement. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy ​said these US actions will hurt Ukraine. Brent crude oil briefly touched $110 a barrel on Friday for the first time since ‌May as ⁠tensions and security threats in the Middle East raised concerns over the safety of shipping and tighter global energy supplies. “The combination of a softer tone around sanctions and some profit-taking after recent gains is helping to cap the upside in the near term,” KCM Trade chief analyst Tim Waterer said. While the US waiver on Russian sanctions ​could lead to higher Russian fuel exports, the mixed messaging has created uncertainty, he added. “Until the details and duration are clearer, the market is unlikely to fully price in ​a sustained increase in supply,” he said. Intensified attacks on commercial vessels cut Gulf crude flows sharply to about 8.5 million barrels per day on a seven-day average last week, from more than 20 million bpd the week before, analytics firm Kpler said in a note on Friday. At least 10 confirmed incidents ⁠involving commercial ​vessels were reported last week, it added. Potentially raising the stakes ​in the Middle East war, Egypt said it is ready to provide Saudi Arabia with the support it needs to defend its security ​and stability against Yemen’s Iran-allied Houthis.

items.title: El Gobierno arranca los “martes sociales” con un decreto para mejorar las prestaciones por viudedad, incapacidad, para víctimas del terrorismo y de violencia de género
items.description: El Gobierno se ha tomado muy en serio la idea que lanzó Pedro Sánchez el mismo día que convocó las elecciones . Esto es, que piensa “seguir gobernando hasta las elecciones”. El martes pasado, el Consejo de Ministros no tuvo mucho contenido político ni decisiones de calado porque era un día especial en el que toda l a actualidad estaba centrada en la visita de los Reyes a Ceuta. Pero a partir de esta semana, el Gobierno, según diversas fuentes, empieza una secuencia que ya no parará hasta las elecciones de lo que se ha llamado internamente como “martes sociales”. Esto se traduce en que en cada Consejo de Ministros se aprobarán medidas que han propuesto los ministerios y que habían quedado pendientes para poder sacarlas adelante antes de los comicios del 29-N. Seguir leyendo

items.title: El Constitucional discute si intervenir ya en la controversia sobre la suspensión del derecho al voto de 160.000 españoles por la ‘ley de nietos’
items.description: “El vínculo entre ser español y el voto es indisoluble”, afirma el Defensor del Pueblo en su recurso de amparo ante el Tribunal Constitucional en defensa del derecho al voto de más de 160.000 españoles que residen en el extranjero y a quienes el Tribunal Supremo ha privado cautelarmente del sufragio. Todos son españoles y el Defensor considera que lo son “pacíficamente incluso para las partes” que recurrieron ante el Supremo —los partidos Vox y Iustitia Europa— quienes “cuestionan solo” una Instrucción del Ministerio de Justicia con indicaciones para la aplicación de la llamada ley de nietos de 2022. Para el Defensor, es “harto problemática” la suspensión del sufragio a los descendientes de exiliados de la posguerra nacionalizados en virtud de dicha ley. Muchos ya votaron en 2023 . Seguir leyendo

items.title: El hospital de Ceuta remite al juez una veintena de partes de lesiones de inmigrantes que dicen haber sido agredidos por militares
items.description: La investigación sobre las presuntas agresiones sufridas por inmigrantes en Ceuta a manos de militares puede dar un vuelco con la documentación que el único hospital público de la ciudad autónoma ha remido al juzgado de guardia. Según ha podido saber EL PAÍS, el centro hospitalario ha puesto en conocimiento de la Justicia al menos una veintena de partes médicos en los que figuran las identidades de las víctimas, las lesiones que presentaban y su declaración de que las heridas fueron causadas por miembros del Ejército que realizaban patrullas de vigilancia en Ceuta . Hasta ahora, las denuncias difundidas tenía carácter anónimo y carecían de informes médicos que las avalaran, lo que abocaba la investigación a un callejón sin salida. Seguir leyendo

items.title: La juventud europea se planta ante un futuro sin salidas
items.description: Decenas de miles de jóvenes han tomado las calles en Francia, Bélgica, España, Italia y Albania. Se suman así a la llamada revolución de la generación Z (nacidos entre 1997 y 2012), que impulsó en los dos últimos años la caída del Gobierno de Bangladés, la dimisión del primer ministro de Nepal y la disolución del Gobierno de Madagascar. Ahora, en Europa, a las puertas de un superciclo electoral , en el que se decidirán los gobiernos de cuatro de los cinco países más poblados de la UE (Francia, Italia, España y Polonia), los jóvenes comparten un descontento generacional marcado por la sensación de que su futuro se vuelve cada vez más estrecho y precario. Seguir leyendo

items.title: C’est non
items.description: Flaubert es insuperable: “De vez en cuando llega una avalancha de mierda y lo sacude todo”, dice el genio con certera escatología sociológica. En las primeras décadas del siglo XXI, esa avalancha tiende a irrumpir después de un proceso de ajustes y reformas , dos eufemismos recalcitrantes de ese detonador sociopolítico que es la palabra recortes . La tijera suele encender una mecha de malestar. En Francia, la novedad es que ni siquiera hacen falta recortes para atizar el fuego: Macron, que llegó cargado de promesas y discursos a lo Kennedy, lleva años sin conjugar verbos como reformar, ajustar y recortar. Y aun así lo tiene todo patas arriba. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Deep Purple: el último solo de una guerra interminable
items.description: El pasado 12 de agosto se vivió un momento que el rock había dado por perdido. Ritchie Blackmore regresó a Deep Purple después de 33 años de ausencia y décadas de peleas con su gran enemigo, el vocalista Ian Gillan. El encuentro fue breve: apenas seis minutos y medio, los que duró la interpretación de Smoke On the Water, con el fraseo de guitarra más famoso del rock duro, obra de Blackmore. Ocurrió en la parada neoyorquina de la gira de 2026 de Deep Purple. “Histórico reencuentro”, tituló Rolling Stone. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Una superviviente de Nagasaki: “La humanidad no ha aprendido la lección de la bomba atómica”
items.description: “Buenas tardes, tengo 84 años y toda mi vida ha estado definida por la bomba”. Mitoe Matsumoto tenía tres años y cuatro meses el 9 de agosto de 1945, cuando a las 11.02 de la mañana estalló sobre Nagasaki la segunda bomba atómica que lanzó Estados Unidos contra Japón al final de la II Guerra Mundial . Se trataba de una bomba de plutonio, más potente que la de uranio, que tres días antes había explotado sobre Hiroshima . Nagasaki no era el objetivo y tampoco el barrio sobre el que fue lanzada. Pero el piloto del bombardero B-29 Bockscar vio un claro entre las nubes y decidió soltar el proyectil, cuyo nombre en clave era Fat Man , contra el valle de Urakami , donde vivía una importante población cristiana, unos cuatro kilómetros al norte del centro de la ciudad. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Puertas cerradas, puertas abiertas
items.description: Desde el primero de septiembre, cada mañana atravieso la plaza del Panteón y bajo hacia el Sena, en dirección al bulevar Saint-Michel, acompañando a mi hija de tres años a la escuela. Ella va en su pequeña bici; a veces viene también el perro. Acaba de empezar la educación infantil. Está descubriendo un lugar donde aprende cosas que por la tarde me contará orgullosa, como quien trae en los bolsillos un tesoro. Pasamos junto a Henri-IV y Louis-le-Grand, los liceos más prestigiosos de París. Desde antes de que naciera, sueño con que algún día pueda estudiar allí. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Odiar Madrid
items.description: Odiar Madrid se ha convertido en un género literario. No uno cualquiera, sino uno de esos que aspiran a conferir prestigio y distinción a quien lo ejerce. Como el haiku o las novelas gordas. Renegar de la capital de España, despreciar su atmósfera o denunciar la hostilidad de sus gentes (así, en plural, como harían Yolanda Díaz o Julio Iglesias) ha pasado a ser una pose pretendidamente chic y cultivada. Odiar Madrid es salirse de la masa ejerciendo de masa, es reivindicarse viajero contra los turistas o defender la civilización frente a la barbarie. Odiar Madrid es elegir lubina cuando crees que todos piden chuletón. Seguir leyendo

items.title: La Comunidad Valenciana y Baleares continúan bajo aviso rojo en la fase más adversa de la dana ‘Adam’
items.description: España se enfrenta a la fase más adversa del temporal de lluvias torrenciales provocado por la dana Adam en conjunción con otros factores , como la entrada de vientos húmedos procedentes del mar Mediterráneo que aportan gasolina a las precipitaciones. A lo largo del día, lloverá con tal intensidad y tal persistencia en la fachada mediterránea y Baleares que se pueden producir, de nuevo, inundaciones y crecidas de cauces. La Agencia Estatal de Meteorología (Aemet) mantiene avisos en seis comunidades, Ceuta y Melilla . Lo más grave se encuentra, por segundo día, en la Comunidad Valenciana y Baleares. La primera continúa bajo aviso rojo ―el máximo― por lluvias y amarillo ―el mínimo de un sistema que contempla tres niveles― por tormentas, viento y mala mar. El archipiélago tiene aviso rojo por lluvias, naranja por tormentas y amarillo por mala mar. Seguir leyendo

items.title: El dueño de Plus Ultra dice al juez que pagaron al “grupo Zapatero” antes de saber si les ayudarían
items.description: “Esperaba que su memoria fuera un poco más fuerte en este tema” o “intente ser un poquito más claro porque si no sospecho que hay algo raro como juez instructor”, son algunas de las frases que José Luis Calama, a cargo del caso Plus Ultra , le espetó al que fuera presidente de la aerolínea y que sigue siendo dueño mayoritario de la compañía. Julio Martínez Sola declaró el pasado 7 de septiembre en la Audiencia Nacional y, durante horas, relató cómo la empresa acudió en 2020 a lo que llamaban “grupo Zapatero” para lograr, presuntamente, que el Gobierno les diera un rescate de 53 millones de euros tras la pandemia. Sola dijo que no le costaba ninguna gestión concreta que el expresidente del Gobierno José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero hubiera hecho en la Sociedad Estatal de Participaciones Industriales (SEPI), pero que “ante la duda” accedieron a pagar el 1% de lo que se suponía que iba a ser el dinero del rescate. La declaración, a cuyo contenido íntegro ha tenido acceso EL PAÍS, discurrió entre la continua incredulidad del magistrado de la Audiencia Nacional porque la compañía no supervisara quiénes eran sus inversores o prestamistas y los reproches por la falta de concreción de las respuestas de Sola. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Conspiración en Badajoz
items.description: Un hombre enchaquetado y con corbata —apostado ante un estantería atestada de libros de donde cuelga una percha con una toga negra y puñetas blancas— se aclara la garganta, toma aire y mira directamente a la cámara. “Hola. Bienvenidos al canal Magistrado Anticorrupción TV. Mi nombre es Luis José Sáenz de Tejada Vallejo y, durante 18 años, he sido juez por oposición”, se presenta en un vídeo subido a YouTube en mayo de 2023. En ese momento, Sáenz de Tejada (56 años) llevaba casi un lustro expulsado de la carrera por una condena a prisión por violencia machista contra su expareja, una magistrada que ejerce en Badajoz. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Las víctimas del ‘caso Magrudis’, la gran intoxicación de listeria en la carne mechada: “Nos destruyó”
items.description: 399840 es el número que Ana Carrillo lleva tatuado en su muñeca desde noviembre de 2019 sobre el dibujo de su mano y la silueta del hijo que estaba gestando entonces. Las cifras se corresponden con el día en que nació sin vida, el 3 de septiembre; lo que midió, 9,8 centímetros, y lo que pesó, 40 gramos. Es la única imagen que Ana guarda de su hijo Mateo, una de las víctimas del brote de listeriosis por la carne infectada de La Mechá, cuyo juicio comenzó este viernes , siete años después de que la Junta de Andalucía decretara la alerta sanitaria. El tribunal ha dado una semana más a las partes para llegar a un acuerdo que evite el macrojuicio en Sevilla. “Me dan miedo las agujas, pero me daba más miedo que se me estaba rompiendo la única imagen que tenía de él, que era una eco de la semana 12 que llevaba en la cartera. Decidí hacerme el tatuaje para llevarlo siempre conmigo, es una imagen del único momento que lo sostuve en mi mano”, explica a este diario. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Miles de afectados por los vuelos anulados de Plus Ultra a Colombia y Argentina: “No nos devuelven el dinero”
items.description: “Hace ocho años que no veo a mi mamá, que está muy mayor. Pedí un crédito en mayo para viajar ahora a Buenos Aires y verla, pero me han anulado el vuelo y no responden a las llamadas ni a los correos. Estoy desesperada”, dice entre lágrimas Viviana Coria, argentina de 52 años y residente en Tenerife. Como ella, miles de personas se han visto afectadas —la compañía no precisa cuántas— por la anulación de vuelos de Plus Ultra de Madrid a Argentina y Colombia . Las rutas a este último país cesaron en junio y muchos de quienes se quedaron sin volar llevan meses esperando el reembolso. Los perjudicados se organizan en grupos de Facebook y WhatsApp para reclamar y denunciar su situación, mientras la aerolínea asegura que ha pagado ya el 78% de los billetes anulados. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Los grandes destinos turísticos tratan de combatir la saturación con nuevas tasas y herramientas de IA
items.description: España se encamina a superar por primera vez los 100 millones anuales de turistas . Ninguna de las señales que apuntaban a una desaceleración se ha cumplido. Entre enero y agosto se superaron los 70,4 millones de viajeros extranjeros, con un crecimiento del 5,4%. Si la tendencia se mantiene, algo bastante posible en función de las reservas que manejan hoteles y agencias de viajes, se podría alcanzar la cifra de 102 millones. Conscientes de que este nuevo escenario es ya una realidad, los destinos más visitados intentan, con poco éxito por ahora, controlar el tránsito de miles de visitantes con el objetivo de que no colapsen la ciudad y puedan tener una convivencia armónica con los residentes. Herramientas de IA y nuevas tasas y cupos se abren paso en el catálogo de soluciones. Seguir leyendo
